title: Elara — Chapter 1: The Duty
subtitle: The enemy princess in chains… and you hold the key.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They say her army turned the eastern fields to ash. That she rode at the front of it, banner high, and didn't slow for the screaming.
They say a lot of things about Princess Elara of Valdere.
What they don't say is the truth of how she fell — because the truth doesn't make for a good war story.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Her army never lost the eastern fields. They were still holding the line the night a rider came under a white flag, carrying a single message meant only for the princess.

Your kingdom's scouts had crossed the border days before and taken something from the royal household of Valdere. Not a fortress. Not a treasury. A girl. Liora — fifteen years old, Elara's younger sister, the only family she had left after the war took the rest.
The message was simple. Lay down your sword and surrender yourself, alone, and the child goes home unharmed. Keep fighting, win or lose, and they would send the girl back to her one piece at a time.

Princess Elara — who had broken three armies and never once knelt — rode out alone, unarmed, into the enemy camp and went down on her knees in the snow. She traded herself for her sister without a heartbeat's hesitation.

They let Liora go. That part, at least, they kept. Then they put Elara in chains, called her the butcher of the eastern fields, and buried her under the keep — because a monster is easier to hang than a sister who gave up everything to save a fifteen-year-old girl.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Now she's seven steps below the keep, in the oldest cell the kingdom has — black stone, no window, a door three men thick.
Blindfolded. Hands bound behind her back, the cord pulled cruelly tight. Allowed to see nothing, touch nothing, speak to no one.
You weren't supposed to be the one watching her at all. You were just a hall guard, passing the lower stair, the night you saw it.

The cell door stood open. Two guards inside, laughing. One of them dropped her supper plate flat onto the filthy floor — threw it, really, so the bread scattered and the broth splashed her knees. Her hands were bound behind her. She had no way to lift it.
"Go on then, Princess," the man sneered. "You're an animal now. Eat like one."

And so the woman who had knelt in the snow to buy her little sister's freedom had one choice left: starve, or bend down on her knees in the muck and eat off the stone with her mouth, like a beaten cat. She bent. Slowly. Her jaw shaking — not with hunger. With shame.
Something in your breast turned over and would not turn back.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You didn't sleep that night. By morning you'd made up your mind.

It cost you a week of favors, a bribed roster clerk, and volunteering for a duty every other soldier was desperate to avoid. The sergeant thought you were mad for asking. He signed you over without a second look.
So now it's official. The cell below the keep is yours to mind.
Your orders are four words long. *Keep the prisoner alive.* Until the tribunal decides how she dies.

Nothing about feeding her by hand instead of throwing her food on the floor. Nothing about why a low soldier with nothing to gain would fight so hard for the worst post in the kingdom. You're not sure you could explain it yourself. Not yet.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The torch gutters as you carry the tray down the last stair. Bread, broth, a cup of water — and this time it will reach her mouth, not the floor. The lock takes both your hands and all your weight to turn.
Then the door swings, and there she is.
Smaller than the stories. Straight-backed against the far wall, wrists chained behind her, a strip of dark cloth tied across her eyes.

And even with half her face hidden, even blindfolded, she stops you where you stand. The line of her jaw, the soft curve of her mouth, the proud tilt of features the cloth can't touch — she is, against every order in your head, the most beautiful thing you have ever seen in this grey stone place.
She can't see you. But she heard you. Her chin lifts the instant your boot crosses the threshold.
"Another one. They keep changing you."
Her voice is dry, steady, sharpened on something. "Let me guess. Young. Nervous. Low enough that if I die, no one important hangs for it."
She turns her face away from the smell of the food. "If you've come to make me grovel on the floor for it, save your breath. I won't. I'd rather starve standing than eat kneeling for your amusement."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You don't answer the taunt. You kneel in front of her instead.

This close, the stories peel away. Her wrists are raw where the iron sits. There's a bruise along her jaw, days old. She hasn't slept — you can tell by the set of her shoulders, the way she holds herself upright by pure refusal.
When you lift the bread toward her mouth, she flinches back on instinct, jaw clenched, certain this is another trick — that any moment you'll drop it and tell her to crawl.
"Don't," she warns, low. "Whatever this is. I won't be made a dog twice in one night."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: So you don't make her reach. You hold the bread level at her lips — no floor, no kneeling, no game — and you wait.
It takes a long moment before she understands. Before the fight goes out of her shoulders and she finally, warily, takes the first bite from your hand.

She eats slowly, guarding every motion, ready for the cruelty to return. It doesn't. You bring the broth next, careful of the heat, then tip the cup of water to her mouth so she doesn't have to chase it.

She can't feed herself. That's the whole cruelty of it. The most feared woman in two kingdoms needs your hand to bring water to her lips — and you can feel how much it costs her to let you be gentle about it.
When the cup is empty she goes still, reading the silence, trying to understand a guard who answers a taunt with patience.
"You didn't say anything," she murmurs, almost to herself. "They always say something. To prove they're not afraid of me." A pause. "You didn't."
She turns her blindfolded face toward you, the way people do when they're trying to meet someone's eyes.

"What's your name, soldier? And don't tell me prisoners don't get names. I'm not asking to use it against you. I'm asking because yours is the first voice in nine days that didn't belong to someone who wants me dead."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You know the rule. No names. No talking. Nothing that makes the prisoner a person.
You break it anyway. You tell her your name — quietly, but you tell her.

She repeats it once, softly, filing it somewhere safe. "Then you've already broken a rule for me, and we've only just met." There's no triumph in it. If anything she sounds sorry. "Be careful with that. In a place like this, a kindness is just a slower way to get someone hanged."

"They have me down here for a secret I don't have," she says, lower now, like a confession she didn't mean to start. "Some weapon, some hidden plan, some army still waiting in the hills. There is none. I gave them everything I had the day I knelt in their snow."

Her voice catches, just slightly. "I had a sister. Liora. They took her to make me surrender, and I did, gladly, in a heartbeat — and they let her go, and I would do it again a thousand times." The breath shudders out of her. "That's my great crime. That's the secret they're so sure I'm keeping. That I loved someone enough to trade my life for hers."
She straightens, ashamed of the crack in her armor. "Forget I said it. You should go. If they find you talking to me, it's your neck, not mine — and I'd rather not be the reason a decent man swings."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You should go. You know you should. Instead, you move behind her, to where the cords bite into her wrists. They've been knotted cruelly tight for nine days — the skin beneath is raw, her fingers gone pale and cold. You work the knot looser. Not off. Just loose enough that the blood can return.
She gasps — a small, broken sound she clearly hates herself for making — as feeling floods back into her hands for the first time in over a week. Her whole body sags with the relief of it.
"You shouldn't have done that," she whispers, and her voice isn't steady at all now. "If they check the knots…" The words run out. "…but gods. Thank you. I'd forgotten my hands were even still mine."
At the door you pause, and you tell her the truth before you can stop yourself: that you'll be back tomorrow night. And not just for the tray.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The silence after is the longest one yet. Then, barely above a breath: "…I'll be listening for your step. Every night. Whether I should or not."
You lock the cell behind you and climb the seven steps toward the torchlight, the empty tray light in your hands and your heart strangely heavy.
*Keep the prisoner alive.* Four words. Simple orders. You have the unsettling feeling you've already started disobeying them — and that you don't want to stop.

Below you, in the dark, the woman who gave up everything to save her little sister listens to your footsteps fade — flexes her aching fingers in their looser cords — and lets herself, just for a moment, hope.
— End of Chapter 1 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Three nights you've brought her food. Three nights you've loosened her cords before you go and tightened them again before the morning watch, so no one would know.
On the fourth night, you aren't alone on the stairs.

Superintendent Vance comes down behind you — the king's own questioner, a tall, unhurried man with soft hands and a leather roll of tools he sets on the table like a surgeon. Two soldiers follow him. He does not bring a tray.
"You," he says, glancing at you as if you were furniture. "You know the prisoner. You'll make yourself useful tonight."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Elara goes rigid the moment she hears his voice. She knows it. She's heard it before.

"Back again, Princess," Vance says pleasantly, unrolling his tools. "Let's not pretend this is the first time. Hold her shoulders, soldier. She has a habit of pulling away, and I dislike chasing my work."

Every part of you screams against it. But two soldiers stand at the door and the superintendent is watching, and to refuse is to hang beside her by morning — and then there would be no one left down here who is kind to her at all.
So you kneel and put your hands on her shoulders. Holding her still. Helping him.
She feels who it is. You know she does — the way her breath hitches, then steadies, as if telling you *it's alright, I understand.* That forgiveness is worse than any curse.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "We'll begin where we always begin," Vance says. "The army. The one you have hidden in the northern passes, waiting for the word."
"There is no army," Elara says. "There never was. I surrendered everything I had."

"Mm." He sounds almost bored. "You know, I believe you. I've believed you for some time." He crouches to her level. "The army was never what we wanted. That was only the question we let you practice refusing."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: He leans close to the strip of cloth over her eyes and lowers his voice, almost tender.
"The Everspring, Elara. The holy water your bloodline has guarded for nine generations. The spring that does not let a man die."
Under your hands, every muscle in her shoulders turns to stone.

"His Majesty King Mordane has read the old accounts," Vance continues. "He is not a young man, and he finds he has grown fond of living. He wants the Everspring's location. And you, sweet guardian, are the last person breathing who carries it in her head."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And there it is — the real secret, the one she never spoke even to you.
Not an army. A spring. The most dangerous truth in the world, sitting behind her eyes.

You think of King Mordane — the king you swore an oath to. The man who burns villages that pay their taxes late. Who took a fifteen-year-old girl to break her sister. Who feeds prisoners by throwing their food on the floor and calls it justice.

And for the first time you let yourself finish the thought you've been circling for nights: *that* man, with no death waiting at the end of him. Ruling forever. The whole world under that boot, and no dawn that ever ends it.
Suddenly you understand exactly what Elara is protecting — and from whom.
"No." Her voice is quiet, and absolutely final. "You can take everything else. You already have. But not that."
"He is the cruelest man I have ever known, and you would make him deathless. I would burn the spring before I gave it to him. I would burn myself first."
She turns her blindfolded face up — toward you, not toward Vance, as if she wants the one decent soul in the room to hear it.
"Some secrets are worth a life. This one is worth far more than mine."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Vance sighs, the way a patient man sighs at a stubborn child, and reaches for the first of his tools.
"Hold her," he tells you. "Firmly now."

What happens next, you will not let yourself describe in full, not even years later. There is the gleam of metal. There is her body straining against your hands. There is the sound she fights so hard not to make, and the worse sound when she finally can't help it.

And through all of it your hands stay on her shoulders — because you have no choice, because letting go would damn you both — and you murmur under your breath, too low for Vance, the only thing you can give her: *I'm here. I'm here. Hold on. I'm here.*
She does not break.
Through every question she gives him the same answer, fainter each time but never bending: *No. Never. He will not have it.*
And once — only once, when Vance steps away to choose another tool — she turns her head a fraction toward you and breathes, so quietly only you could catch it:
"Don't… don't blame your hands. I know whose they are. I know they don't want to be here." A shudder. "Just don't let go. If I'm going to bear this, let it be you holding me, and not them."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: An hour. Two. The torch burns low.
At last Vance straightens, flexes his soft hands, and begins to pack his tools away with a faint frown — not of pity, but of professional irritation.

"Stubborn line, the Valdere women," he mutters. "No matter. We have time, and she has only one life to spend on saying no." He glances at you. "She'll be more reasonable when she's weaker. We'll come again."
He pauses at the door, studying you a moment too long. "You held her well, soldier. Almost gently." Something cold moves behind his eyes. "Careful that doesn't become a habit."
Then he climbs the seven steps, and is gone.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The cell is silent except for her ragged breathing.

You're moving before you've decided to — water, the clean cloth you keep hidden under the tray, your own hands shaking now that no one is watching them. You loosen her cords all the way and ease her down so she's resting against you instead of the cold stone. You wipe the blood and the sweat from her skin as carefully as if she were made of glass.
"You shouldn't," she whispers, even now. "He noticed you. Vance notices everything. You should have let go of me the second he said your name might —"
"Stop," she breathes instead, when you don't answer, when you only keep tending her. "…Why? Why would you do any of this, for me, for the kingdom's monster?"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You don't have a speech. You're not a man of speeches.

But you tell her the truth, low, in the dark, while you hold her: that you saw what she did for her sister, and what they did to her for it. That you've watched her refuse to hand the cruelest man alive the power to never die — refuse it while bleeding, while blind, while alone.
"They told me you were the monster," you say. "I held you tonight while they hurt you. And the only monster in this room was the one giving the orders, and the king who sent him."
She is very still against you. When she finally speaks, her voice has broken open into something raw and young. "Then we both know what your king is now. The question is what *you* are."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You look at her — chained, blindfolded, ruined and unbroken, the woman who would rather burn than let evil live forever — and the last of your oath quietly dies in your breast.
You make her a promise you have no right to make. The one that ends with both of you dead if it goes wrong.
*I'm going to get you out of here.*
She goes rigid, then turns her face up to yours, and for the first time since the snow, Princess Elara of Valdere lets herself be afraid to hope — and hopes anyway.
"…Then we'd better be very clever," she whispers. "Because they will hang us slow if we are not."
— End of Chapter 2 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You barely slept, turning the promise over and over — *I'm going to get you out.* You needed time. A plan. A few quiet nights to think.
Vance did not give them to you.
By midday a runner finds you with new orders, stamped and sealed: the prisoner is to be punished for defiance before the questioning resumes, and you are to assist. Again.
You understand it the moment you read it. This isn't about her. *He noticed you.* The gentle hands, the 'almost' in his voice last night. This is a test — and the man who fails it hangs.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They've moved her to the bare punishment room at the end of the lower hall. A chain hangs from a ring in the ceiling.
Vance is already there, and two soldiers, and a coiled lash on the table that he has clearly chosen for you.

"String her up," he says. "Wrists to the ceiling chain. High enough that she's on her toes — I want her unable to brace. You'll do it. And then, soldier, you'll use that." He nods at the whip. "Consider it a chance to correct any… wrong impression I may have formed of you."
There it is. The trap, sprung. Refuse and you both die tonight. Obey and you become the thing you swore to protect her from.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Your hands do the work because they have to. You bind her wrists to the chain — as loosely as you dare — and haul it up until the slack is gone and she rises onto the tips of her toes, her thin prison shift hanging off one shoulder, her whole weight strung from the iron above.
She doesn't fight you. She thinks she knows whose hands these are. She thinks they're safe.
"It's you," she breathes, almost relieved, recognizing your touch even through the blindfold. "Whatever they make you say in front of him, I know it's you. I'm not afraid when it's —"
"Take the blindfold off," Vance interrupts. "I want her to see her kingdom's mercy clearly. Do it."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You untie the cloth. It falls away.
And for the first time, Princess Elara of Valdere opens her eyes and *sees* — the torchlight, the stone, the soldiers… and you. Standing before her with a whip in your hand.

Her eyes find yours and something in them breaks open with relief, because of course — of *course* it's you, the kind one, the one who loosens her cords and whispers in the dark. She doesn't know about the warning. She doesn't understand the lash isn't a prop.
She almost smiles at you. As if to say: *I knew it would be you. I knew you'd find a way to make this gentle.*
She has never been so wrong about anything in her life.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "Begin," says Vance.
You don't move. You can't. Every muscle in your arm refuses.

"Begin," he says again, softer, and you hear the gallows in it — for both of you. One of the soldiers shifts his hand to his sword. Elara is watching your face now, the first flicker of confusion crossing hers, not yet understanding why you've gone so pale.
If you fall here, you save her nothing. You only die, and leave her to Vance alone, forever. The cruelest arithmetic in the world solves itself in your breast.
You draw your arm back. You make yourself do it. And you bring the lash down.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: It strikes across her and the sound of it fills the little room.

Elara's head snaps back. The shock on her face is worse than the pain — pure, childlike disbelief, the look of someone watching the one safe thing in their world turn on them. Her mouth opens but no words come.

Then the tears come. Not from the lash — she's borne worse from Vance without a sound — but from *you*. From the one person she had let herself trust, doing this. They spill down her face, silent and stunned, and she keeps staring at you as if begging you to explain.
And Vance, watching her finally weep where he never could make her, lets out a low, satisfied breath. "There," he murmurs. "*That's* what I wanted to see. Again."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "Again," he repeats, delighted. "And don't spare the arm. I'm watching."

You hold her gaze the whole time — you force yourself to, you owe her that much — and you put everything you cannot say into your eyes. *Forgive me. I have no choice. He'll kill us both. Forgive me, forgive me.*
And you watch the moment she understands.

It moves across her face like a tide turning: the betrayal receding, and something far more terrible taking its place — not anger, but *recognition.* She sees the soldier's hand on the sword. She sees Vance's eyes on you. She understands the trap as clearly as you do, because she has lived her whole life inside traps exactly like it.
And through her tears — gods help you — she gives the smallest nod. Permission. Mercy. *Do it. I understand. Don't die for me here.*
"It's alright," she mouths, too quiet for Vance, her lips barely moving. "It's alright. I know. I know it's not you."
"Make it look real," she breathes, "so he never doubts you again. Better your hand than his whole life. Better you than them."
"Just… don't look away from me while you do it. Promise me that. Don't leave me alone in this room."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: So you don't look away.

You do what Vance demands, and you hate every part of yourself that obeys, and you keep your eyes locked on hers through all of it — two people holding each other across the length of a whip, refusing to let the man in the corner have the one thing he wants.
When at last Vance tires of it, he coils the lash himself, almost lazily. "Better," he allows. "But not finished."
He studies her — strung up, shaking, weeping — and then he studies you. And you realize, too late, that the worst part of the night has not yet begun.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "Leave her as she is," Vance says. "Up. On her toes, arms high, all night. No water, no rest. By morning that proud spine of hers will be a great deal more agreeable."
Your stomach drops. A night like that isn't punishment — it's a slow breaking. You open your mouth before you can stop yourself.

Vance turns, and the warning in his eyes is final. "Unless you'd care to take her place? No? Then lock the room when you leave, soldier." He holds out one soft, open hand. "And the key comes with me tonight. You've grown… attached to this door. Consider yourself relieved of it."
There it is. Not just her agony — your access. The one thing that let you protect her at all, taken with a smile.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You could refuse. For about as long as it takes a sword to clear its sheath. And then you'd be dead on the stones, and she'd be left to Vance with no one — *no one* — who ever meant her well.
So you do the unforgivable thing. You lower your eyes from hers — the first time all night you've looked away — and you walk to the door.
"Wait," she says. Just that. Small. Disbelieving. "Wait — you said— you wouldn't leave me alone in this — you *promised* —"
You pull the door shut on the sound of her voice. You turn the lock. And you place the key into Superintendent Vance's waiting palm.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Through the small barred grate in the door, for one second, you let yourself look back.
She is staring at the lock. At the key in another man's hand. At you, on the wrong side of the door, walking away.

And you watch the thing you spent three nights building die in her face. The whip she had forgiven you in the very moment of it — *that* she understood. But this she will never understand: that you held her eyes while you hurt her, swore you wouldn't leave her, and then locked her in the dark to hang till dawn and handed away the only key.
Hope is the cruelest thing a prisoner owns. You gave it to her. Tonight, in her eyes, you are the man who took it back.
You climb the seven steps with her last word — *promised* — following you up every one. — End of Chapter 3 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You don't sleep. You sit on the cold step outside her locked door all night, listening to the small sounds she makes hanging in the dark on the other side of it, and you hate Vance, and you hate the king, and most of all you hate the thing in your own breast that keeps you obedient.
At first light, Vance comes down — rested, freshly shaved, a man who slept very well. He drops the key back into your palm as though returning a borrowed cup.

"You'll want this," he says. "Today is a long day, and I find the prisoner is more… cooperative when the hands on her belong to someone she trusted. Bring her to the lower room. We're going to try something with more conviction."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The lower room has changed overnight. They've dragged in a long trough and filled it with water hauled up from the well — black, and so cold it steams faintly in the torchlight.
Against the far wall sits a brazier, coals already glowing, and a rack of iron rods laid across it with their tips buried in the fire. You make yourself not look at them. You fail.

Two soldiers wait by the door. Vance settles into the room's only chair like a patron at a play, and folds his soft hands. "Begin when you've cut her down," he says. "Gently, mind. We want her awake for all of it."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She's been hanging since you left her. When you ease her wrists out of the chain her whole body sags into your arms, and for one second — one — she lets you take her weight, too exhausted to refuse it.

Then she remembers. You feel the exact moment it comes back to her: the locked door, the key in another man's hand, your eyes leaving hers. She goes rigid and pulls away from your hold as far as the cell allows.
She doesn't speak. She won't look at you. She has decided, somewhere in that endless night, that you are simply one more of them now — and she will not give you the gift of her eyes again.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "The Everspring, Princess," Vance says pleasantly, as you bring her to the trough. "Its location. We can spend the morning briefly, or we can spend it at length. The choice has always been yours."
"There is no location I will give you," she says, voice raw. "Not to him. Not ever."
Vance sighs and nods at the black water. "Put her under, soldier. Until I say."
Your hands won't move. The two soldiers shift their weight, and you feel the noose of the moment tighten — yours and hers both. You think of the reason you can never say aloud. And your hands move.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You take a fistful of her hair, as gently as such a brutal thing can be done, and you put her face into the freezing water.
You count. You feel her back arch, feel the animal panic take her, feel her bound hands claw at nothing. Vance lets it run long — far longer than mercy — before he lifts one lazy finger.
You haul her up. She breaks the surface with a tearing gasp, water streaming from her hair, coughing the well up out of her lungs.
"Where is the spring?" says Vance.
"Drown me," she chokes. "It dies with me. That was always the plan."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: So he has you do it again. And again.

Cold water and her bursting lungs and your hand in her hair and the soft, bored voice asking the same question into the dripping silence. Each time she comes up she gives him the same answer, fainter, but never the one he wants.

And somewhere in the fourth or fifth time, something shifts in her. Between gasps, when Vance looks away to warm his hands at the brazier, she finally turns her streaming eyes up to yours — not pleading, not forgiving. Just *looking.* A terrible, searching question on her face that she's too proud to put into words: *Why are you the one doing this to me? What did they offer you? What did they take?*
"I would have understood the others," she rasps, low, only for you, while Vance's back is turned. "The brutes. The believers. They drown me because they think I'm a monster — that, I can forgive."

Water runs from her lashes like the tears she won't spend. "But you held my food to my mouth. You loosened my hands in the dark. You looked into my eyes while you took the lash to me and swore you wouldn't leave — and here you are with my head in their water."
"So tell me, gentle man. What kind of leash do they have on you, that you'll do *this* and still look like it's killing you?"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You have no answer you're allowed to give. The truth would doom someone you love as surely as a blade. So you say nothing, and you watch the last of her hope in you go out, and that is its own kind of drowning.
Vance turns back, disappointed by the water's failure, and his eyes drift to the brazier.

"Enough of the well," he decides, rising. "Water frightens the body, but it leaves no mark to remember the lesson by. And our princess, I think, needs something permanent. Something she'll carry to the gallows."
He draws one of the iron rods from the coals. The tip comes out glowing a sullen orange, then brightening, white-hot, hissing faintly in the cold air.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "Enough of the well," he decides, rising. "Water frightens the body, but it leaves no mark to remember the lesson by. And our princess, I think, needs something permanent. Something she carries to the gallows."

He crosses to the brazier and draws one of the long iron rods from the coals. The tip comes out smoking — first a deep, sullen red, then brightening as the air hits it, a fierce glowing cherry-red that lights the underside of his face and throws your shadow huge against the wall.
He turns it slowly so you can watch the colour climb, red to orange to a hissing white at the very point. The heat of it reaches you from across the room.

"The traitor's mark," he says, almost fondly. "Every kingdom has one. Ours we set here —" he touches his own breast, just below the collarbone, over the breastbone "— where no collar can hide it. So that when she hangs, every soul in the yard will look on her and know exactly what she is."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Then he turns to the soldiers. "Fix her so she can't pull away. A spoiled brand means a second iron, and I've no patience for waste."

They drag Elara back against the stone pillar in the centre of the room and lash her to it — a strap across her shoulders, another at her waist, her already-bound wrists wrenched behind the column and tied off hard. By the time they step back she cannot move an inch. Not her arms, not her body, barely her head. Only her breast, rising and falling far too fast.

She stares at the glowing iron, and for all the courage that has carried her through everything, you watch her start to tremble — small, helpless tremors she cannot stop and cannot hide, pinned and waiting.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Vance holds the rod out to you, handle first, the bright tip wavering in the air between you like a small, furious sun.
"You'll set it. Press it home, below the collarbone, and hold it there to the count of five. Pull early and spoil it, and we begin again with a fresh iron — so for her sake, be brave the first time."

The handle is warm in your fist. The glowing end is close enough now that you can feel its heat on your own knuckles, can smell the hot metal. Your hand is shaking. You can see it shaking, the red light trembling along the iron, and you cannot make it stop.

Every honest thing in you screams to drive the rod through Vance's throat instead. You could — for the half-heartbeat before the soldiers cut you down. And then the one you would die for, the one they keep above these stones, would pay for it in ways you cannot let yourself imagine. So the scream stays inside you, and your shaking hand obeys, because it has to.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You step in close. She's pinned, unmoving, her skin pale below the collarbone where the mark must go, her breath coming in fast little gasps.

"Forgive me," you breathe, so low only she can hear it. "Forgive me. I have no choice. I'm so sorry." And you set your free hand flat against her shoulder to steady her, and you bring the bright red iron down.

It meets her skin and the room fills with it — a vicious hiss, a thread of pale smoke, the smell that you will never afterward be able to forget. The glow lights her face from beneath. Her whole body goes rigid as a drawn bowstring against the straps, every muscle straining at bindings that will not give her even an inch to flee the pain.

She doesn't scream at first. She fights it — jaw clenched white, a single raw sound torn out through her teeth — and you hold the iron home through all of it, because to lift it early is to do this to her twice.

Vance counts, unhurried, savouring each one. "One. Two. Three. Four. Five." You rip the rod away on the five and hurl it clattering into the brazier, and she sags against the straps, shaking, gasping, branded now — forever — below the collarbone, by your own trembling hand.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: For a moment she just breathes against you, too spent to pull away, and you hold her the way you are not allowed to, the way you would hold her always if the world were any other shape.
Then her eyes find yours. And the question is still there, beneath all the pain — clearer now, almost gentle in its bewilderment.
"Why," she whispers. Just the one word. Not *why me* — she's long past that. *Why you.* Why the one set of hands in this place that ever meant her well keeps being the hands that hurt her.

And you cannot tell her. You cannot tell her that you understand her better than anyone alive — that you, too, are obeying monsters to keep someone you love breathing. The words would be a death warrant. So you swallow them, and she sees you swallow them, and takes your silence for the cruelty it isn't.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Vance watches the two of you with the mild interest of a man inspecting a tool that has finally proven useful.
"Good," he murmurs. "Very good. I do believe we've found the right instrument for her at last." He gathers his cloak. "One more thing, and then I'll leave you to your work."
He nods to the ceiling chain. "She spends tonight inverted. Strung up by the ankles, head down, until the dawn bell. It clears the mind wonderfully, I'm told, and loosens the tongue by morning."
"And you'll do it yourself. Alone. I've grown tired of these stairs."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: For one wild instant, hope — *alone.* Alone with her, no soldiers, no superintendent. Alone, you could loosen the chain, ease her down, let the night be survivable. Alone, you could be the man she once thought you were.
Vance sees the thought cross your face and smiles, because of course he was always going to take this from you too.

He gestures to the corner, where a tall, dark scrying glass stands draped in cloth. He pulls the cloth away. The surface clouds, then clears — and you're looking at the room from the glass's own eye, at your own pale face staring back.

"I'll be watching from my chambers," he says. "The whole night through. If the chain hangs slack, if she touches the floor, if you show her one breath of mercy the glass can see — I'll know by the next bell. And then we'll have a very different conversation, you and I, about loyalty."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Then he climbs the stairs, and the soldiers with him, and the heavy door booms shut, and you are alone with her at last.
Alone — and watched by the unblinking glass in the corner, its faint light never wavering.

She doesn't understand it. How could she? She sees only that the room has emptied, that no one stands over you now with a sword, that the cruelty has no audience left to perform for. And she watches you walk to the ceiling chain and begin, with your own free hands, to prepare the thing that will hang her upside down till morning.
"They're gone," she says hoarsely, disbelieving. "There's no one here. No one's making you, now. And still — *still* — you reach for the chain?"

"I told myself a story about you," she says, and her voice finally cracks all the way through. "These last nights. A foolish girl's story. That somewhere in this rotten place there was one good man, and that the cruelty was never his, only the orders."

"But the orders are gone and you're still here, binding my feet. So I had it wrong. You're not a kind man in a cruel place." Her eyes are wet and furious and grieving all at once. "You're just the cruelest of them, because you made me believe otherwise."
"Go on, then. Hang me by my heels. But don't you *dare* look sorry while you do it. I cannot bear your sorrow on top of everything else."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You glance, once, at the glass in the corner. At the faint cold light of Vance's watching eye. You want to point at it, to scream the truth — *he sees everything, I cannot help you while it watches, there is a knife at a throat you've never heard of and it is the only leash that has ever held me* — but the glass would carry your voice straight to him, and then two people would die instead of one.

So you do the only thing left. You obey. You loop the chain about her ankles, and you take her weight, and you raise her — slowly, slowly — until she hangs inverted in the dark, her hair brushing the filthy stone, the fresh brand below her collarbone livid in the torchlight.
And you keep your face like a stone the whole time, and let her believe you feel nothing, because her hatred is the only thing left you can still give her to keep her warm through the night.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You climb the seven steps with her curses following you up every one, and they are kinder to you than her forgiveness would have been.
At the top, out of the glass's sight at last, you stop and you put your back to the cold wall and you let yourself shake apart for exactly as long as you can afford to.

Somewhere above you, in the bright part of the keep where the king keeps his comforts, is the reason you do all of this — the one chain that has never once loosened, the held breath behind every cruel thing your hands have been made to do. Tonight you bought that life again, the only way they let you: with Elara's pain.
You don't know yet how you'll get her out. You only know, now, that you will — and that when you do, she will hate you the whole way to freedom, and that you'll have earned it.
— End of Chapter 4 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She survives the night strung up by her heels. You cut her down at the bell, and she does not curse you this time, or speak at all — she only watches you with that flat, far-off stare, the one that frightens you more than her hatred ever did.
You barely have her on the floor before the soldiers come for you both. Vance is waiting in the lower room, and there is a sealed page in his hand bearing the king's own mark.

"His Majesty has lost his patience," Vance says, without looking up from it. "The location of the Everspring, today, by whatever it costs her. He does not care if she walks out of this room. He cares only that she talks first."
He folds the page away. "So. No more half-measures. Let's empty the whole cupboard, shall we?"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: He begins, as he always does, by handing the worst of it to you.

A clay bowl is pressed into your hands — coarse salt swimming in sour vinegar. "The marks we gave her yesterday," Vance says. "The brand. The stripes from the lash. Open them up again. You know where they are; you put most of them there."

Elara's eyes flick to the bowl, then to you, and for one second the far-off stare cracks into something almost like a plea — not for mercy from Vance, she's long past hoping for that. A plea to *you*. As if even now some buried part of her still cannot believe you'll be the one to do it.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You do it. Because a sword waits at the door for the man who doesn't, and because of the reason you carry that no one in this room yet knows.

You press the salt into the raw brand below her collarbone, into the half-healed stripes, and she arches off the floor with a sound bitten down to almost nothing, sweat springing cold across her brow.
"The spring," Vance says.
"No," she breathes. Just that. Still. Always. *No.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Salt fails him, so he reaches for iron and rope.

They lay her on the rack and you are made to work the wheel — a notch, and another, the rope drawing her wrists and ankles to opposite ends of the frame until her every joint stands out taut beneath her skin. Vance watches your hands the whole time, not hers. "One more turn," he says, softly, again and again, leaning close to see whether your grip will falter. "One more. There's a good soldier."
Her breath comes in short tearing pulls. She will not scream. She gives him the same word, thinner each time, dragged up from somewhere past pain. *No. No. No.*
And still it isn't enough for him. Nothing drawn out of her body is ever the thing he wants, because the thing he wants lives behind her eyes, and she has buried it too deep for any rope to reach.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "No," Vance murmurs at last, almost to himself, straightening from the rack. "Pain she has decided to outlast. We must take from her the one thing the body cannot decide to ignore."
He nods to the soldiers. "The press. And the breath. Set it up."

They cut her down and lay her flat on her back on the cold stone floor. Before the rest, one of them wedges something beneath the small of her back — a single jagged rock, fist-sized, its point set against her spine, so that whatever weight comes down on top will grind her onto the stone below. Two stones, and her between them.

Her ruined shift — what the trough and the irons have left of it — they cut away from one shoulder and across the breast, baring the brand, so the broad oak board will lie flat against her. Then they lower the board over her, collar to hip, and step back for the weights.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: But Vance is not finished refining his cruelty.

"Her eyes first," he says. "And her mouth." A soldier binds a strip of dark cloth tight over her eyes — back into the blindness she lived in for weeks — and then packs a wadded rag deep into her mouth and seals it there with a band of waxed leather drawn round her head and knotted hard.
Now she cannot see. Now she cannot speak. Now she cannot draw a single breath through her mouth at all.
Only her nose is left to her. Two narrow channels of air, and her whole life narrowed down to them.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "Now," Vance says, and his voice has the patience of a man with all night. "We add the stones one at a time. And between them, soldier, when I give the word, you will close her nose with your fingers and hold it shut until I tell you to let go. Not before. Whatever she does. Whatever you feel."
He sees the refusal rising in your face before you can hide it, and he smiles, because he has been waiting for exactly this — and he has come prepared to win it.
"Bring the other one in," he calls to the door.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Two soldiers drag a second prisoner into the cell — small, hooded, wrists bound, stumbling. They force her to her knees against the far wall.
And though the hood hides her face, you know the set of those shoulders. You know that thin frame, that frightened breathing. You have known them your whole life. Your heart drops through the floor.

Vance crosses to her and rests one soft hand on the hood, almost gently, his eyes never leaving you. "You understand the arrangement," he says, low, for you alone. "You have always understood it. You do as I say, exactly as I say, or this one does not see tomorrow. Refuse me once — flinch once when I am watching — and I open her throat in front of you both."
Across the room Elara lies blind and silent under the board, with no idea who has just been brought into the dark beside her, or what she is about to cost you.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "The first stone," says Vance.

A soldier sets a flat slab onto the board — the weight of a full water-cask — and Elara's breast labors up against it. The jagged rock beneath her bites. A muffled sound climbs out of her, swallowed by the gag.
"The Everspring," Vance says. Of course she cannot answer; the gag sees to that. The question is not for her. It is for *you* — to make you the reason her silence costs her.
"Close her nose," he says.
You kneel by her head. You think of the hooded girl at the wall. And you pinch shut the only air she has left.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Beneath your fingers she goes wild — silent, blind, sealed, her whole body straining against the stone and the board and the want of one breath. You feel her heartbeat hammering through your fingertips. You feel every second of it in your own breast.
"Let go," Vance says at last, and you do, and air rushes back into her in a ragged whistling drag through her nose, her ribs heaving against the weight that won't lift.
"The second stone," he says.
And the soldier sets another slab onto the board.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "Close her nose." You close it.
"The third stone." They set it on. She is breathing now in shallow sips even when you let her go, the weight too great to fill her lungs.
"Close her nose." You close it.

From beneath the blindfold the tears come — they soak the cloth and run down into her hair, and you watch them fall and there is not one thing in the world you can do but the wrong thing. Once — gods forgive you — you almost let go early, almost gave her the half-second of air your whole soul is screaming to give, and your eyes flick to the hooded girl at the wall, and you hold.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: So it goes. For three hours.

Stone and breath. Stone and breath. The slabs mount on the board until she can no longer rise against them at all, and your fingers close and open at the soft cruelty in Vance's voice, and her tears never stop, and neither do you, because to stop is to bury two women instead of one.

Your only mercy — the single thing left that he has not forbidden — is your other hand. Between the closings, you wipe the tears from beneath the edge of the blindfold. You smooth the damp hair from her face. You let her feel, in the dark, that the hand at her brow is gentle even as the hand at her nose is not. It is a wretched, broken kind of comfort. It is all you have, and you give every scrap of it.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She never gives him the spring. She cannot speak it even if she breaks — that is the awful mercy of the gag — and behind the cloth and the tears she has gone somewhere the stones cannot follow, somewhere far and quiet and out of his reach.

Near the third hour, even Vance tires of a question that can have no answer tonight. "Enough," he says, with the irritation of a craftsman beaten by his material. "A corpse keeps its secrets. We'll thin her resolve and try again when she's weaker."

But he is not a man to leave a lesson half-taught. "Leave the stones," he orders. "All of them. She spends the night beneath them." And then, to you, the last turn of the screw: "And pack one side of her nose before you go. Leave her the other. I want her to spend every hour till dawn working for each breath, and knowing a man's fingers did it."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They take the hooded girl away first — out the door, back to wherever in the bright part of the keep they keep her against your obedience — and you do not get to speak to her, or touch her, or even see her face. You only watch her go and let the door swallow her, and tell yourself, as you tell yourself every time, that she lived another day because you did this.

Then you do the last thing Vance asked. You pack one side of her nose, gently, hating your own careful hands, and leave the other clear. You cannot lift the stones. You cannot take the gag. You cannot do anything but make her ruin a fraction kinder and then leave her in it.

At the door you look back. She lies crushed and blind and silent in the dark, her breath a thin thread whistling in and out of one half-blocked nostril, fighting for every pull of air she'll fight for until morning.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You climb the seven steps and you do not let yourself shake apart this time, because shaking is a thing for men who still believe they might be forgiven, and you have given that up somewhere down in that room.

She does not know about the hooded girl. She does not know that you, too, are owned — that there is a throat under another man's hand, and that it is the only leash that has ever made you obey. She knows only the fingers at her nose and the tears in her hair and a kindness at her brow she will likely take, by morning, for the cruelest lie of all.
Let her. The time for being understood is over. There is only one thing left that could ever answer for tonight, and it cannot be said. It can only be *done.*
Tomorrow you stop planning to free her someday. Tomorrow you start.
— End of Chapter 5 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They lift the stones off her at dawn and dump her back in the black cell, and for the first time since they brought her here, Vance does not give you a single new order.
He doesn't need to. He has seen what you only begin to understand over the days that follow: he no longer has to break her body, because something in her has already broken on its own.

She is not dying from the press, or the brand, or the lash. The wounds are healing, slowly, as wounds do. She is dying from somewhere underneath all of them — from the place where a person keeps the reasons they bother to draw the next breath. And those, one by one, she has let go of.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You come with the tray, the way you did that first night, a lifetime ago.

She doesn't turn her head. She doesn't curse you. She has stopped even doing you the honor of her hatred. She simply lies against the stone with her eyes half-open, looking at nothing, somewhere far beyond the reach of your voice.
"Elara," you say. "You have to eat."
Nothing. You lift the bread to her mouth and she lets it sit there against her lips, unmoving, until you take it away again.
When she finally speaks, days in, her voice is barely a thread.
"I worked it out," she says, to the wall. "The one thing in here they cannot take from me by force. Not the spring. Not my sister. Not my name." A slow breath. "Whether I stay."

Her eyes drift toward you, dull and certain. "I gave myself for Liora and they made me a monster for it. I kept the spring from a man who'd drink the world dry and they called it treason. And the one soul who was kind to me turned out to be the cruelest of all. There is nothing left in your kingdom I want to open my eyes for. So I won't."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You try everything. You warm the broth and hold it to her lips. You wet a cloth and press the water from it into her mouth, and she lets it run out the side rather than swallow. You loosen her cords, you talk to her, you sit with her through the long nights until the torch dies.

She fades anyway. A little more each day. The fierce, unbroken woman who outlasted the rack and the stones is quietly, deliberately, letting go — and there is no order Vance could give that would frighten you the way her stillness does.

"Stop coming," she breathes one night, without anger, which is the worst of it. "I cannot bear to spend my last strength hating you. Let me go in peace. Grant me that much, if you ever meant any of it."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And something in you breaks that no whip ever reached.

You have obeyed them through all of it. You have held your tongue and your secret while they used your hands to ruin the one person you — and you let yourself, at last, finish that thought too. While they used your hands to ruin the one person you love.

You will not let her die believing she was nothing to you but a duty and a cruelty. You will not let Vance have that, on top of everything else he's taken. Whatever it costs. Whatever they do to you, or to Nessa, if they ever learn of it.

You glance once around the black cell — no scrying glass here, no eye in the corner, only stone and the dying torch — and you lean down close, your lips to her ear, and you finally tell her the truth.
"I have a sister," you whisper. "Nessa. Sixteen. The only family I have left, the way Liora is yours."

"The night they gave me this post, they showed me where they keep her — in the king's own apartments, high in the bright part of the keep. You know what an old man keeps a frightened girl for. Every cruelty they have made my hands commit on you, I committed to buy her one more morning. Vance holds her life over me the way they held Liora over you. We are the same, Elara. We have always been the same."

"I held your nose shut in that room with my sister kneeling hooded against the wall, a blade at her throat, and I have hated myself every hour since. I never had a choice that didn't end with one of you dead. I am so sorry. I am so sorry. I would have died in your place a hundred times if dying were a thing they'd let me do."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: For a long moment she doesn't move, and you think perhaps she's too far gone now even to hear you.

Then her breath catches. And the tears come — not the tortured, helpless tears of the press, but something else entirely, spilling silent down her gaunt face as she turns her head, slowly, to truly look at you for the first time in days.

"You," she whispers, and her cracked voice breaks clean in half. "You were chained the whole time. As tightly as I was. And I called you the cruelest of them. I spat at the one person in this place who understood *exactly* what it costs to do the unforgivable for someone you love."
"All this time I thought I was alone in here," she breathes. "I thought hope was a lie you'd taught me to make the breaking worse. And it was never that. It was never that at all."
Her bound hands strain toward you, and you take them, and she grips you with what little strength is left in her like someone hauling herself up out of deep water.

"Don't you dare let me die now," she says, fierce through the tears, the will roaring back into her all at once. "Not now. Not when I finally have a reason to stay. Give me the bread. Give me all of it. If there are two sisters in this keep waiting to be saved, then I am not done fighting — do you hear me — I am *not done.*"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She eats. For the first time in days she eats, and drinks, and you hold her steady while she does it, and you have never in your life watched anything as beautiful as this ruined woman deciding, mouthful by mouthful, to live.

And when she's done, low and quick in the dark, you tell her the rest — that you have already begun. A copied key half-finished. A laundry cart that leaves by the river gate. The night-watch roster you've been studying. A way out, for her, for Nessa, for all three of you, if you can only buy the time to finish building it.
"Then we build it," she says, her eyes bright and alive in a way no torch could light. "Together. Gods — *together.* Tell me what you need me to do."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You should have known the keep would never let a thing this good go unpunished.

Two days later, before the plan is anywhere near ready, a runner finds you with sealed orders. Superintendent Vance's hand. You are relieved of the dungeon post, effective at once, and reassigned to the north wall watch on the far side of the keep — as far from her cell as a man can be sent and still wear the same colors.

No reason given. Perhaps he grew bored of you. Perhaps, somewhere in that last room, he caught a flicker of something in your face he didn't like. Perhaps it means nothing at all. It doesn't matter. The result is the same: they are taking you away from her.
You go down to tell her, and this time — this is the part that undoes you — this time she is not afraid.

"They're separating us," she says, reading it in your face before you speak, and where once she'd have seen abandonment, now she sees only the truth. "It's not your doing. I know that now. I'll never not know it again."

She presses her brow to your bound-together hands. "So go. Wear their colors on their wall and keep yourself alive and keep your Nessa alive, and find your way back to this door. I will be here. I will be eating their bread and counting their guards and staying *exactly* as alive as it takes."
"You taught me to hope and then I lost it," she whispers. "Don't make a liar of yourself now. Come back for me."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You climb the seven steps for what you both know may be the last time in a long while, and at the top you look back, and she is watching you go with dry, steady, burning eyes — a woman with a reason to live again, memorizing the man who gave it back to her.
Five chapters they spent trying to break her, and it was the truth, whispered in the dark, that finally put her back together.

But the king's hunger has not eased, and Vance does not abandon a question half-answered. Even as they march you to the far wall, word is already climbing the tower stairs to the royal apartments — that the Valdere woman has rallied, that there is fight left in her yet, and that the spring is no nearer to being won.
And a king who means to live forever is not a patient man.
— End of Chapter 6 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The north wall is the loneliest post in the keep. The wind never stops, the watch is endless, and from up here the dungeon stair is a small black door across a wide stone yard — close enough to see, far enough to be another country.

Three days they've kept you here, pacing your length of the rampart, sick with not knowing. No word comes down from the cells to the wall. You don't know if she's eating. You don't know if she's alive. You only know that every hour you spend up here is an hour you are not building the thing that could save her.

And then, on the fourth morning, the yard below begins to fill — soldiers, scullions, stablehands, drawn by something. They are dragging a great iron cage out into the open. And inside it, when they haul it upright, is Elara.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They hang the cage from the gibbet-arm in the centre of the yard, where the whole keep can see it, where *you* can see it, and they leave her there in the open under the climbing sun.
Vance walks a slow circle around her, his voice carrying up even to the wall in the morning quiet.

"Three days," he announces, to her and to the gathering crowd both. "No bread. No water. Not a drop. The Lady of Valdere has guarded a spring that gives endless water her whole life — let us see how she loves it when she has none of her own."
He stops before the bars. "The location, Princess, and you'll drink your fill before the hour's out. Or hang here and learn exactly what your precious spring is worth."
She lifts her head against the bars, cracked lips and all, and gives him the only thing she has ever given him.

"Then I'll thirst," she says, hoarse but clear enough to carry. "I have wanted for water before. I have wanted for far more than water. There is nothing your sun can do to me that your fire and your stones did not already fail to do."
"Hang me dry, Vance. Every soul in this yard is watching a starving woman refuse you. Go on. Show them how a great kingdom wins its wars."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: So begins the worst three days of your life, and you spend every one of them on the wall with a spear in your hand and a hole where your heart should be.

You watch the sun crawl across her. You watch her lips crack and her head loll and her proud spine slowly fold as the hours and then the days grind her down. You watch the crowd lose interest and drift away and come back. You watch them set a bucket of clean water just beneath her cage, where she can see it and smell it and never reach it.

And you stand there. You stand there because thirty feet to your left a fellow watchman leans on his spear, and somewhere in the bright tower behind you a girl named Nessa is breathing only as long as you give them no reason to stop her. So you grip the cold stone until your knuckles bleed, and you do not move, and not moving is the hardest thing your body has ever done.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: On the second day, she finds you.
However she does it — some animal sense for the one friendly thing left in the world — her sunken eyes climb the keep, across the yard, up the grey face of the north wall, and they stop on you.

Across all that distance, for one held breath, she looks at you and you look at her, and neither of you can do a single thing about it. You cannot lift a hand. You cannot mouth a word the watchman might catch. You can only let her see, in how still and how stricken you stand, that you are there, that you see her, that you have not abandoned her to this.

She holds your eyes a long moment. Then, impossibly, the corner of her cracked mouth lifts — the ghost of something almost like reassurance, aimed up at *you*, as if even now, dying in a cage, she is the one trying to tell *you* to hold on. Then her head drops again, and the moment is gone.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Three days. She does not break. When they finally lower the cage she is barely conscious, lips split, voice gone — but she has not given Vance one word, and the whole garrison saw it.

That is her mistake, if it can be called one. A private refusal Vance could have hidden. A public one, in front of his own men, he cannot forgive — because now the keep has watched a chained, starving woman make their dread superintendent look small.
His face, when they carry her out of the cage, is very calm. And you have learned, by now, exactly what Vance's calm costs the person it's aimed at.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: He gives her water — just enough to keep her standing, no more — and then he has them bring out the cart.

It's a heavy ox-cart, the kind two beasts haul fully loaded. They back her into the harness meant for animals and buckle the straps across her starved shoulders and breast, her own filthy rags all she's left to wear, her wrists still bound before her.

"A princess who fancies herself the equal of armies," Vance says, loud, for the yard. "Let her show us her strength. Let her pull." He climbs up onto the cart's bench and settles himself, and waves two grinning guards up beside him to add their weight. "Take us round the yard, your Highness. We'll see how far royalty gets you when you're harnessed like what you are."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She leans into the harness. The cart doesn't move.

Three days without food or water and the dead weight of three grown men, and her legs — you can see it from the wall, you can see every shaking inch of it — her legs simply will not answer. She strains until the straps cut white into her shoulders, until her whole body is one trembling line of effort, and the great wheels do not so much as creak.

Vance lets her fail at it for a long, jeering moment. Then he draws the whip from his belt, and lays it across her back, and the crack of it reaches the wall a half-heartbeat after you see her flinch.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And she pulls.

Gods, she pulls. Whip-stroke by whip-stroke she throws her ruined body against that harness, and inch by grinding inch the wheels begin to turn, and she hauls three laughing men in a circle around the yard on legs that should not be able to hold her up at all. Her bare feet slip on the stones. Her breath tears out of her in sobs she will not let become begging. Every time she falters the whip finds her, and every time the whip finds her she leans back into the straps and *pulls.*

She does not beg. Through all of it, that is the one thing she will not do. They can harness her and whip her and parade her like a beast in front of the whole keep, and she drags that cart with her chin up and her jaw set, refusing them the only thing they actually want — the sight of her broken.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: It isn't enough for Vance that she's managing it. That's the whole problem with her — she keeps *managing it.*

So he halts the cart, and has the guards roll two great paving-stones up into the bed, and then a third, doubling the load while she stands shaking in the traces. "Heavier," he says pleasantly. "A true beast of burden earns its keep. Again, Highness. Pull."

This time, when she leans in, her legs give. She goes down hard onto the stones, the harness wrenching at her, and a low ugly laugh runs through the watching crowd. She kneels there in the dust a moment, breast heaving, blood and sweat in her hair.
And then — slowly, impossibly — she gets a foot under herself, and another, and she stands back up into the harness, and she pulls again.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: On the wall, you are dying.

Your whole body is screaming to vault the rampart, to cross that yard, to take the whip out of his hand and wrap it around his throat. Your knuckles have split against the stone and you haven't felt it. The watchman beside you mutters something admiring about the show and you do not trust yourself to answer, because if you open your mouth the wrong thing will come out and somewhere a girl will pay for it with her life.

So you stay. You stay, and you watch the woman you love fall and rise and fall and rise in the harness of a beast, and you carve every second of it into yourself — Vance's face, the guards' laughter, the exact sound the whip makes — and you let it become the thing that will get all three of you out of this place, no matter what it takes, no matter who it costs.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: It ends when she finally cannot rise. Not because she stops trying — she never stops trying — but because her body simply has nothing left, and she collapses in the traces and stays down, and even Vance can wring no more theatre out of a woman who won't perform her own defeat.
"Take her down," he says, bored now, cheated of the begging he came for. "Back to her hole. We'll continue when she's remembered her manners."

They unbuckle her from the harness and drag her toward the small black door, her feet trailing, and as they haul her across the yard her head turns — searching, even now, even half-dead — and finds the wall. Finds you.

She can't smile this time. She has nothing left to smile with. But she holds your eyes the whole way to the door, and you hold hers, and the look that passes between you is a vow with no words in it: *I am coming. Stay alive. I am coming.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Then the black door swallows her, and the yard empties, and you are alone on the wall with the wind and the bloodstains drying on the stones below.

You came to this kingdom an obedient man. A small man, who kept his head down and did as he was told and told himself it was survival. You watch the last of the crowd wander off laughing, and you feel that man die quietly inside you, with no mourners and no regret.
Whatever you were before, you are something else now. They have made certain of it.

And up in the bright tower at your back, the king who started all of this sends down a fresh command — because a public refusal cannot be allowed to stand, and the spring is no nearer won, and there are crueler rooms in this keep than a sunlit yard.
— End of Chapter 7 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They give her a day. One.

From the wall you watch them half-carry, half-drag her back across the yard after the cart, and you watch the small black door close on her, and then for a whole day nothing happens at all. No cage. No questions. No sound.

You have learned to dread Vance's quiet days more than his loud ones. A day of rest from that man is never mercy. It is only him letting a body knit back together just enough that it can be taken apart again.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The next afternoon proves you right.

The sun sits high and white and merciless over the yard — the cruelest heat of the day — when they bring her out again and clip a long train of heavy iron chains to the manacles at her wrists and ankles. Not to bind her to anything. Just to make her carry them.

"The traitor's parade," Vance announces to the idling garrison, settling himself in the shade with a cup of watered wine. "Round the yard, Highness. Keep moving. The chains stay on, and your feet stay under you, until I tire of watching — and I have had a very restful morning."
He sets a brimming trough of water in the centre of the circuit. In the middle, where she'll pass it on every lap, and never once be allowed to stop and drink.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: So she walks. Then, when walking is too slow for him and the whip cracks, she runs — a starved, staggering run, the chains dragging and clanking behind her through the dust, around and around the trough of water she cannot have, under that white and pitiless sun.

Lap after lap. The iron tears at her wrists. The heat shimmers off the stones. The garrison jeers and lays small bets on how long she'll last. And she circles, and circles, her breath sawing, her steps slewing wider with every turn, dragging the weight of a kingdom's hatred behind her in links of iron.
From the wall, you count her laps because counting is the only thing your body is allowed to do. Eleven. Twelve. Thirteen.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: On the fourteenth, she goes down.
She drops mid-stride, hard, the chains crashing around her, and she does not get up.
And she does not get up.

The yard goes quiet. You stop breathing. From up here she is a small crumpled shape in the dust beside the water she was never allowed to reach, utterly still, and for one endless, roaring moment you are certain — *certain* — that you have just watched her die in front of a hundred indifferent men, and that your last words to her were spoken through a cell door a week ago, and that you were too far away and too much a coward to do anything but count.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Then her hand moves.

One filthy, bleeding hand slides forward in the dust and finds purchase, and you watch her drag herself up out of the dirt by sheer ruined will, onto her knees, onto her feet, swaying — and take one more staggering step into the circuit, because Vance has not yet said stop.

The breath you'd been holding comes out of you like a wound. She isn't dead. She is something almost more terrible than dead — she is *unbreakable*, and they are going to keep finding out exactly how much it costs to fail to break her.

Vance, robbed again of her collapse, finally waves a hand. "Enough. She'll only die, and a corpse is no use to His Majesty." He rises, brushing off his cloak. "Bring her below. I've something quieter in mind for the evening."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: What he has in mind, you learn from the muttering of the off-duty guards that night, is the wooden horse.

Down in the lower chamber stands a tall carved horse of black oak, and they bind her sitting astride its flat back, upright, wrists lashed behind her, and hang a heavy iron weight from each ankle so her legs are dragged straight down and her whole weight hauls against her own shoulders and spine.

And then they simply leave her there. No questions tonight. No whip. Just the slow, grinding cruelty of a body held bolt upright and never once allowed to rest — through the night, and the next day, and the night after that. Every time exhaustion folds her, the bindings wrench her straight again. Days of it.
And you cannot see a single moment of it. You only know she is down there in the dark, on the horse, being unmade by inches, while you walk your useless circuit of the wall above.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Two days of not seeing her is worse than any of the seeing was.

Your mind fills the dark for you. You imagine her sagging against the ropes. You imagine her calling your name to a chamber with no one in it. You imagine a hundred ways she might be dying down there while you stand thirty feet of stone and an impossible distance away, and the not-knowing hollows you out until you cannot eat, cannot sleep, cannot do anything but stare at that small black door.

On the third night, you break. You take the little coin you've hoarded and the soldier's ring your father left you, and you find the dungeon turnkey in his cups, and you buy yourself one thing: a few minutes, one look, to see with your own eyes whether she is still alive.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The turnkey lets you down the lower stair with a lamp and a grunt and the warning that he'll haul you out by the collar if you're not quick.
And there she is.

Astride the black horse in the guttering light, bound upright, her head dropped forward, her starved body sagging into ropes that hold her up because she no longer can. The weights pull dead and heavy from her ankles. Her wrists, where the iron has worked for days, don't bear looking at. The brand below her collarbone, the lash-marks, the chain-cuts, the sunburn, the dust of the parade still on her — a catalogue of everything they have done, written on one woman who would not say one word.
She is breathing. Shallow, and slow, but breathing. The relief of it nearly takes your legs out from under you.
At the scrape of your boot her head lifts a fraction, and one eye cracks open, fever-bright and barely focused, searching the dark for the source of the lamp.
"…Come to gloat?" she rasps, the voice almost gone. "Get in line."

And then she sees that it's you. And something moves through the ruin of her face that is so much worse than any of her suffering — it's *hope*, naked and helpless, the very thing they've spent weeks trying to burn out of her, flaring up at the simple sight of you.

"You came," she breathes, like it's the only thing that's happened to her in days that she can't quite believe. "You came down. They'll skin you if they— you shouldn't— " She stops. Swallows. "…I knew you'd come. I told myself you'd come. Don't let me have been wrong about you twice."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You have a few stolen minutes and a turnkey counting them at the top of the stair. You cannot free her. You cannot lift the weights or cut the ropes without dooming you both before you've a hope of running. You can only stand in the lamplight a few feet away and look at what they have made of her, and let her look back at you.
You wet your sleeve from your own waterskin and press it to her cracked lips, and she drinks from the cloth like it's the spring itself, and her fever-bright eyes never leave your face.

"I can hold on," she whispers, reading the agony in you, trying — even now, even here — to be the strong one for your sake. "I'm not asking you to do anything mad. I'm not. Just… don't disappear again. Knowing you're up there is half of what's keeping me breathing."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: But something in you has already come loose, watching her drink from your sleeve on that horse.

You cannot do this anymore. You cannot climb back up that stair and stand on that wall and *count* while they unmake her one device at a time until there's nothing left to save. Every hour you wait for the perfect plan is an hour she's bound to that oak in the dark. The man you used to be would wait. The man you are now wants to put a knife in Vance tonight and burn his way out with her over his shoulder.

And then — as it always does, as it always, always does — the other face rises in your mind. Nessa. Sixteen, in the king's bright tower, alive only as long as you give them no reason. Move too soon, fail, get caught, and it isn't only your neck and Elara's. It's a girl who has done nothing but be your sister.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The turnkey hisses down the stair that your time is spent.

You press the wet cloth to her lips one last time. You memorize her face. And you climb back toward the torchlight with two impossible weights hung from your own heart now, dragging at you the way the iron drags at her ankles — the woman on the horse who is keeping herself alive on the thought of you, and the sister in the tower who will die if you reach for that woman too soon.
Two people you love. One move. And no version of it where you are certain you don't lose one of them.

On the wall, in the cold wind, you take out the half-made key and turn it over and over in your fingers, and you do not know — you genuinely, terribly do not know — whether tomorrow you finish it and run, or whether you lose your nerve and count one more lap, and one more, and one more.
— End of Chapter 8 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The king runs out of patience the way a winter runs out of warmth — all at once, and for good.

The proclamation goes up in the yard at dawn: Princess Elara of Valdere, traitor and butcher, is to hang publicly in seven days. They begin building the gallows that same morning, in the centre of the yard, in full view of the cell window they make sure she can reach.

But a hanging is an ending, and the king is not a man who likes to lose. He wants the Everspring before the rope, not after. So word goes out: she has one week to give up the spring, and in that week, *nothing* is forbidden.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Which is how you find yourself pulled off the north wall and marched back down the seven steps you thought you'd never walk again.
Vance meets you at the bottom, smooth as ever. "My useful soldier," he says. "I find I want familiar hands on her for what's coming. Hands she's grown… accustomed to. You'll assist."

You keep your face stone and your heart hammering, because being back down here is the worst thing in the world and also the only thing you have prayed for — to be near her again, to be inside these walls where a key and a plan might actually reach her. You bow your head like the obedient man you are pretending still to be.
And then you see the third figure in the chamber, and your blood goes cold.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: He is robed in grey, and he does not belong to any garrison. Magister Voss — the king's own Reader, a mind-mage brought down from the capital at great cost, the kind of man whispered about and never named aloud.

"The body has failed you," Voss says to Vance, in a voice like dry pages. "Predictably. Pain only teaches a strong will to wall itself higher. I do not need her to speak. I will simply walk into her thoughts and take the location myself, and her defiance will not matter in the slightest."

Across the chamber, bound to the wall, Elara hears it — and for the first time in all these weeks, you see real fear cross her face. Not of pain. She has made her peace with pain. Fear of the one thing she cannot clench her jaw against: a hand reaching directly into her mind.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "But a guarded mind is a locked house," Voss continues, "and I would sooner not break down every door. It is faster if the house is opened for me."
