He turns his pale eyes on you. "You. The apothecary keeps a stillroom off the lower stair. There is a draught — moonsbane, valerian root, a measure of dreamer's cap — that quiets the watchman of the mind and lets the doors swing wide. Brew it. Strong. To my measure exactly."
He recites the recipe like scripture, and Vance jerks his head for you to go, and just like that they have handed you the one thing in all this you can actually touch.
Because *you* are the one who will mix it. And no one in that chamber knows herbs better than the man they've sent to fetch them.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: In the stillroom, alone, your hands finally have something to do besides shake.

You measure the moonsbane to a third of what Voss asked. You crush the dreamer's cap and tip most of it into the slop bucket. You bulk the cup with plain valerian and well-water until it looks and smells exactly like the thing he wants and is, in truth, little more than bitter tea — enough fog to satisfy a watching mage that the draught is working, nowhere near enough to open the doors of a mind like hers.

And while you're there, among the apothecary's stoppered chaos, your eye catches a small blue vial marked with the sleeper's mark — a strong sleeping draught, the kind that drops a grown man in moments. You think of gate-watches and night-guards and a plan that needs exactly this, and you palm it into your boot before you can talk yourself out of it.
Your first true theft. Your first true act of war. It feels less like fear than you expected. It feels like finally beginning.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You bring the cup back and hold it to her lips yourself — and for half a second your eyes meet hers over the rim, and you will her with everything you have to understand: *trust me, drink, it isn't what they think.* Whether she reads it or simply trusts the hand, she drinks.

A dreamy heaviness settles over her, her head lolling, her eyes going soft and unfocused. To Voss it looks like victory. He steps in close, lays his fingertips against her temples, closes his eyes, and begins to walk into her mind.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You watch the mage's face, and you watch hers, and you hold your breath for a small eternity.

Voss frowns. His fingers press harder. Whatever shallows he's wading through — the snow, a child's laughing face, a soldier's grey eyes she lingers on longer than she should — none of it is the thing he came for. The deep vault where she keeps the spring stays shut, because the draught that should have swung it wide is bitter tea, and the will guarding it is the strongest thing in the room.
Long minutes. Sweat on the mage's brow now. And at last he pulls his hands away with a hiss of frustration.
"It's no use," Voss snaps. "The draught was weak — useless — her mind is still walled to the rafters. I cannot pass without it. Brew it again, properly, or do not waste my—"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "There is no time to brew it again," Vance says, and his voice has changed.

For the first time since you have known him, the smoothness is gone. The king is on his neck, the clock is running, his clever mage has failed, his every device has failed, and the woman bound to the wall is *still looking at him* with that maddening, unbroken calm — and something in Superintendent Vance, at long last, cracks.

He dismisses Voss with a snarl. He sheds his fine coat. And he takes down from the wall a fresh whip, flexing it between his soft hands, and crosses to her with a look you have never seen on him before — not the cold craftsman anymore, but a man who has been made to feel small and intends to take it out of someone's skin.
"Her back is ruined," he says, to no one. "We'll see how the front suits her."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: What follows is not interrogation. He barely asks the question anymore. It is simply rage, with a whip at the end of it.

He lashes her across the front — over the half-healed brand, over the tender places no torturer with patience would choose — and where his earlier cruelties were measured, this is not. Each stroke lays a fresh red weal across her, and she cries out now, truly cries out, the screams torn out of her one after another until the small chamber is full of them.

And still — gods, *still* — between the screams, when he stops to demand the spring, she gives him nothing. Tears stream down her face and her body twists against the bindings and she sobs with the pain of it, and she will not, will not, *will not* say the word he wants. She has named her own death already. There is nothing left in his whole arsenal that can frighten a woman who has nothing left to lose.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You stand against the wall where they've put you, and you are made to watch, and watching is its own whip.

Every stroke that lands on her lands somewhere in you. Your nails are in your own palms. Your jaw aches from holding it shut. You think about the sleeping vial in your boot and the half-made key and Nessa in the tower, and you do the arithmetic of murder a hundred times in the space of a minute — and a hundred times the answer comes back the same: not yet, not like this, not in a room with three armed men and your sister's life in the balance. So you watch. You watch the woman you love weep and scream and refuse, and you let it carve you hollow, and you make yourself a promise with every single stroke.

At last Vance's arm tires before her will does. He steps back, breathing hard, sweat-soaked, beaten by a bound and bleeding woman in front of his own men, and that humiliation curdles into one final cruelty.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "String her up for the night," he pants. "Arms over her head, to the hauling rope. High — up on her toes, so she can't rest, so every breath pulls on what I've given her." He flings the whip down and points at you. "You. Haul the rope and make it fast. Since you're so very good with her."

It is the old trap, the same as the first night, and there is no more refusing it now than there was then. You take the hauling rope. You loop her wrists. And you draw it up — as slow, as gentle as you dare, hating your own hands — until her arms are stretched above her and she rises onto the tips of her toes, the night's whole weight of her hanging from her shoulders, her whipped front bared to the cold chamber air.
You tie it off. You cannot do anything else. Vance watches you do it, satisfied, and then he and his men climb the stairs and leave you the duty of the dark.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They post you to guard her through the night — the final little cruelty, you think, until you realize it might be the only mercy in the whole wretched day. Because it means that for these few hours, the only eyes on her are yours.

There is nothing you can do for her. You cannot lower the rope; the watch above would hear the change and check. You cannot tend the welts; a fresh dressing would be seen by the morning guard. You can only stand a few feet away in the guttering torchlight and witness her — strung on her toes, marked and shaking, weeping in a low exhausted way that has long since stopped being about the pain.

And she weeps like that the whole night through. Not loudly. Just steadily, endlessly, the tears of someone with no strength left to stop them, while you stand vigil over a suffering you would give your own life to end and are not permitted even to touch.
Once, in the deepest part of the night, she lifts her head and finds you in the dark.

"Don't look so broken," she whispers, and even now, even like this, she is trying to comfort *you.* "I'm still here. They didn't get it. We didn't let them, you and I." A shudder of breath. "Whatever you're carrying in those eyes — whatever you're deciding — I see it. I've seen it for days."

"Six nights, they've given me," she breathes. "Six. If you are going to do the mad, beautiful, impossible thing I can see you working yourself toward — do it before the seventh. That's all I ask. Don't let the last thing I see be a rope in a yard. Let it be you."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And there, in the dark, with her hanging on her toes and weeping and still finding breath to give *you* courage, the last of your hesitation finally dies.

No more counting laps. No more waiting for a perfect plan that will never come. There is a sleeping draught in your boot and a half-cut key in your quarters and six nights on the clock, and somewhere above you a sister you will not leave behind either. You don't have a finished plan. You have a deadline, and a reason, and at last the will to spend everything you are on both.
"Six nights," you say back to her, so low it's barely sound. "Then hold on for five of them. On the fifth, I'm coming for you. For all of us."

She doesn't smile — she hasn't the strength. But something steadies in her weeping, something settles, and you both turn your faces to the long dark and begin, separately and together, to wait for the fifth night.
— End of Chapter 9 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You cannot wait for the fifth night. Not with her hanging on her toes by day and the gallows growing in the yard by the hour.

So on the second night after the sentence, you move early — not the whole escape, not yet, but the first and most fragile piece of it. Before you can run with Elara, you have to have Nessa in hand, because you will not buy one sister's freedom at the cost of leaving your own behind.

The sleeping draught is in your boot. You know the watch rotations on the tower stair by heart. You climb toward the bright part of the keep with your heart in your throat, toward the small high chamber where they have kept your sister all these months.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The door is unlocked. That is the first wrong thing.

You push it open on a room that is simply… empty. The narrow bed is stripped to the boards. The little washstand is bare. The shutter hangs open to the night and the cold comes through it unanswered. The room where Nessa has slept and wept and survived for half a year has been cleared out as though no one ever lived in it at all.
Your stomach drops through the floor. You go from corner to corner like a man searching for a heartbeat, refusing what your eyes are telling you. *Gone. She's gone.*

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Then your knee knocks something half-under the bedframe, and you snatch it up.

It's her ribbon. The faded green one she's worn in her hair since she was a girl, since before any of this, since back when you were just a brother and she was just a sister and the worst thing in the world was a scraped knee. It's been left behind in the clearing-out, or dropped, or — you can't tell — left on purpose, by her or by someone crueler.
And scratched into the soft stone of the windowsill, fresh, in the uneven letters of someone working in a hurry and the dark, three words: *THEY KNOW. RUN.*
Nessa's hand. Nessa's warning. Even taken, even terrified, her last thought was to warn you.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "She has lovely handwriting, your sister," says a voice from the doorway. "For someone so frightened."

You turn, and Vance is leaning in the frame, perfectly at ease, two soldiers behind him in the passage. He has been waiting for you. Of course he has. You walked up here following a hope, and the hope was bait, and you swallowed it whole.

"I'll confess I wasn't certain," he says, almost warmly. "One hears things. A guard who looks too long at a prisoner. A draught that fails for no reason a sober apothecary can name. I am a careful man, so I tested it. I moved the girl, and I left the door open, and I waited to see who in all this keep would come climbing to an empty room in the dark."
He spreads his hands. "And here you are. So. Now we both know exactly what you are."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Every muscle in you coils to fight or run, and Vance watches you do the math and shakes his head, almost kindly.

"I wouldn't. The men on that stair are only the ones you can see. And your sister —" he lets the word land "— is somewhere in this keep you will never find in time, in the care of men I have chosen for their lack of imagination. You take one step you shouldn't, and word travels faster than you can run, and she pays it. Do you understand me? She pays everything."

He pushes off the door frame and steps into the bare little room. "But I haven't come to arrest you. A traitor in the dungeon is no use to me. I've come because you have just become the most useful man in this entire keep."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "I have been a fool," Vance admits, pacing the empty room. "Weeks of irons and stones and that idiot mage, all wasted, because I kept trying to take something from a woman who has already given up everything she has. You cannot frighten the dead. Elara of Valdere stopped fearing for herself a long time ago."
He stops, and turns, and fixes you with those flat patient eyes.

"But she has not stopped fearing for *you.* I have watched her watch you. Whatever grew between the two of you in that cell, it is the one live nerve left in her whole ruined body. And you have handed me the way to press on it."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "So here is how the next days will go," Vance says. "My men will go to work on your sister. Slowly. Thoroughly. For as many days as it takes."

"And *you* will go down to the princess, and you will tell her exactly what is being done to your Nessa, in detail, and you will get down on your knees in front of the woman you've grown so fond of, and you will *beg* her for the location of the Everspring. Beg her to save your sister's life with a single word."

His smile is the worst thing you have ever seen. "She watched her own kingdom burn rather than give it up. Let us see if she can watch *your* family burn the same way. Let us see whether the great unbreakable Elara breaks at last — not for her own pain, but for yours."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And there it is. The cruelty so complete it takes your breath.

He has turned the only good thing left in this place — what you and Elara are to each other — into the blade he means to gut you both with. If she holds the line, you must stand and watch your sister tortured for it. If she breaks to save Nessa, then the cruelest man alive drinks from a spring that makes him deathless, and a thousand future Elaras suffer forever under a king who can never die.

And you are the lever. Not a guard anymore, not a torturer's hand. The wedge driven straight between the woman you love and the cause she has given everything to protect. Every word out of your mouth from now on is a betrayal of one of the two people you would die for.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "You'll have until the execution," Vance says, moving to the door. "Six more days. Use them well. Be persuasive. Weep, if you like — I find she responds to your distress, and the more real it is, the better."

"And do not imagine running. There is no plan now, soldier. There is no fifth night. Your sister is hidden where your little stolen key and your little stolen draught can't reach her, and the moment you stop being useful to me, she stops being useful to keep alive. You belong to me now, more completely than you ever did. You'll do this, and you'll do it well, because the alternative is two funerals instead of one."
He's gone before you can answer, and the soldiers with him, and you're left alone in your sister's emptied room with a faded green ribbon crushed in your fist.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You don't know how long you stand there.

Every road out has closed at once. You cannot run — you don't know where Nessa is, and the trying would kill her. You cannot fight — the keep would bury all three of you. You cannot refuse the task — refusal is Nessa's death sentence. And you cannot *do* the task — because doing it means kneeling before Elara and asking her to damn the world to save your blood, and whichever way she answers, you lose something you cannot live without losing.

Vance has built a machine with no exit in it. For the first time since that very first night on the lower stair, you cannot find the next move. There isn't one. There's only the long walk down the seven steps tomorrow, and the worst thing you have ever been ordered to do waiting at the bottom of them.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You uncurl your fist and look at the ribbon. *They know. Run.* She tried to save you, even then. Nineteen years old and being dragged into the dark, and her last act was to warn her brother off.

You will not run. But you make her a promise anyway, there in her empty room, the same one you made Elara on the wall, the same one you seem doomed to keep making to people you cannot reach: *I am coming. Both of you. I don't know how. I don't know how. But I am coming, and I will tear this whole rotten keep down to its foundations before I leave either of you in it.*
Then you put the ribbon in your breast pocket, over your heart, next to the half-made key that is suddenly worth nothing at all — and you go to face the longest six days of your life.
— End of Chapter 10 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They come for you at first light on the first of the six days.

Not to the dungeon — not yet. They march you instead to a windowless room off the guardhouse, plain and cold, and the moment the door opens your heart stops, because there, bound to a post in the centre of it, is Nessa.

Six months since you've laid eyes on her. She's thinner, paler, her dress torn and filthy from wherever they've been keeping her — but she's alive, and whole, and when she sees you her whole frightened face crumples with a relief so total it nearly puts you on your knees.
"You came," she breathes, the same words Elara once said in the dark. "I knew you'd— I told them you'd come for me, I told them—"
"Quiet," Vance says, almost gently, stepping from the corner where you hadn't seen him. "Save your strength, child. You'll want it."

He lays a hand on a thin length of rattan resting on the table — a cane, supple and cruel. "Your brother and I have an arrangement. The princess has a secret she won't part with, and pain hasn't moved her, and threats haven't moved her. So we're going to try something new. We're going to give her a reason that isn't about her at all."
He picks up the cane and holds it out to you, handle first. "Twenty strokes. You'll deliver them. And then you'll go and tell the princess exactly what you've done, and beg her to make it stop."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The room tilts. "No," you hear yourself say. "No. Take me instead. Whatever you want done, do it to me, I'll—"

"You misunderstand," Vance says, unbothered. "Hurting you accomplishes nothing. The princess can watch you suffer all day; you're a soldier, it's expected. But you, hurting *her* —" he nods at Nessa "— that's a thing the princess will not be able to bear, because it will not be able to bear it in *you*. That is the entire point. Now take the cane, or I hand it to a man who will enjoy it, and we make it forty."

And there it is again. The same arithmetic that has owned you since the first night. Twenty strokes from your hand, as soft as you dare make them — or far worse from someone else's, with you helpless to spare her a single one.
You take the cane. Your hand is shaking around it.

And Nessa — gods, Nessa — twists her head around against the post to find your face, and when she understands what's about to happen, she doesn't scream or curse. She does something far worse. She steadies.

"It's alright," she says, through her tears, her voice trembling but certain. "I scratched the warning. I know they made you. I know it's not you, the same way it was never you with her." She swallows hard. "Better your hand than theirs. Do it. I can take twenty. We're stronger than they think, you and I. We always were."
She turns her face back to the post and sets her shoulders and waits, nineteen years old and braver than she should ever have to be, and it is the single hardest thing you have ever had to look at.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You make the first stroke as light as you think you can get away with. It isn't light enough to spare her and Vance's eye is on you and a stroke too gentle means he takes the cane and the count starts over, so it lands, and a thin line of fire blooms across her back through the torn cloth, and she jerks against the post with a sharp, bitten cry.
"One," Vance counts.

You make yourself do the second. The third. Each one tears a little more of the brave silence out of her, until by the fifth she is crying openly, and by the eighth the cries have become small involuntary pleas — *please, please* — not to you, not really, just the body begging the world the way a body does when it hurts and cannot make the hurting stop.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Halfway through she finds your eyes again over her shoulder, streaming, and even now — even now — she tries to give you something to hold onto.
"Keep going," she gasps. "Don't you dare stop and make it forty. I'd rather— ah— I'd rather all twenty from you than one more minute of *him.* Stay with me. Count them with me. We're almost—"

Whatever she means to say breaks apart on the next stroke. You count them in your head with her, the way you counted laps from the wall, the way you seem doomed to count the suffering of everyone you love: twelve, thirteen, fourteen, each number a small private apology that will never be enough.
Vance watches it all with the serene attention of a man confirming a theory.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: At twenty you drop the cane like it's burned you and you're at the post before you've decided to move, fumbling at her bindings, catching her as she sags off the post and into your arms.

She's shaking all over, her back a lattice of welts through the torn dress, but she's alive and conscious and the first thing she does — the *first thing* — is grip your sleeve and whisper, "See? Twenty. Told you. We're alright. We're alright."

"Touching," says Vance, retrieving his cane. "Take her back," he tells the soldiers, and they peel her out of your arms while she's still trying to reassure you, and the door closes on her, and you're left with the superintendent and the smell of blood and the long walk still ahead of you.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "Now," Vance says, brushing off his coat. "The second half of your day. Down you go, to the princess. Tell her what you did. Spare her no detail — I'll be asking the guards what you said, so make it honest. And then beg."

"And understand the shape of this thing, so you don't waste your breath or hers. Today was twenty strokes. Tomorrow is worse, and the day after worse than that, and on it climbs, every single day, until either she gives me the Everspring or the week runs out and we hang her anyway and start fresh on your sister for the sport of it."
He smiles. "You have six days to talk her into saving a life. I suggest you're persuasive."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The seven steps have never felt longer.

Elara is where they keep her now between torments — down from the horse for the moment, slumped against the wall, wrists bound, lifting her head at the sound of your boots the way she always has. Then she sees your face, and the blood that isn't yours on your sleeve, and the thing you're carrying behind your eyes, and her own expression changes.
"What did they do," she says. Not a question. "What did they make you do."

And so, because Vance has left you no other road, you kneel down in front of her, and you tell her. About Nessa. About the post and the cane and the twenty strokes and your own hand delivering them. You watch each word land on her like a blow of its own.
When you've finished, Elara is silent for a long moment, and when she speaks her voice is very low and very steady, and you can hear what it costs her to keep it that way.

"So that's his game," she breathes. "He couldn't break me with my body, so he'll break me with yours. With hers." Her eyes close. "He's cleverer than I gave him credit for. There is no torture he could invent for my own flesh that would touch me like the thought of that girl under a cane because of my silence. None."
She opens her eyes and looks at you, and they're wet, and fierce, and full of a grief so large it has no bottom. "You're going to beg me now. He told you to. So beg. Get it over with. Ask me."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And you can't. You kneel there with your sister's blood on your sleeve and the words Vance ordered you to say stuck in your throat, because to truly beg her — to mean it — is to ask her to hand the cruelest man alive the power to never die, and you have seen exactly what that man does with power, and some part of you that is better than your fear will not let your mouth form the plea.

"I can't," you whisper instead. "He told me to beg you and I— Elara, I can't ask you to give it to him. I've *seen* him. If a man like that never dies—" Your voice cracks. "But she's my sister. She's nineteen. She warned me to run and I didn't and now she's— and I don't know what I am if I let her— I don't *know* what to do. For the first time in my whole life I don't know what to do."
You bow your head, and the soldier and the princess both watch a grown man come apart on a dungeon floor.
Elara doesn't answer right away. When she does, she leans forward as far as her bonds allow, until her brow nearly touches yours, and her voice is the gentlest thing in that whole black place.

"Listen to me. You will not beg, and I will not break — not today. Not yet. We are cleverer than this man, the two of us, and we are not going to let him win by panicking on the first day of six." A breath. "Your sister bought you time with her courage today. Don't spend it on despair. Spend it thinking."

"Six days," she whispers, the words you keep trading back and forth like a coin. "He's given us six days to find a third road — one that isn't my silence killing her or my secret damning the world. There's always a third road. Help me find it before the last of them runs out."
You climb the steps that night with nothing solved and everything to do, and behind you in the dark, for the first time, the princess is not waiting to die. She is beginning, very quietly, to plan.
— End of Chapter 11 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Day two. They came for you before the torches had even been changed, and they did not take you to Elara's cell.

They took you to the stripped room — bare stone, a drain in the floor, and in the center a long iron trough brimmed full of water so cold a skin of ice had formed at its edges overnight. Vance was already there, sleeves rolled, unhurried. And bound to a stool beside the trough, in the same torn shift they had left her in, was Nessa.

Your sister. Nineteen years old. Her wrists lashed behind her, her lips already grey-blue from a night in this cold, her eyes finding yours across the room with a terror she was trying so hard, for your sake, to swallow.

"Good. The brother." Vance didn't look up from the water. He trailed two fingers across the iced surface as if testing soup. "I considered the cane again. But marks heal, and marks make a man angry, and an angry man is stupid. Cold is cleaner. Cold leaves nothing for a magistrate to see and everything for a brother to remember."
He finally turned to you, and his voice was almost kind.

"You're going to put her under. Not me. You. Every time I ask a question and don't like the silence, your hands go on her, and her face goes in the water, and you count to ten while she drowns a little. And when you can't bear it anymore, you'll go down those stairs and you'll make your princess understand that the only way to dry your sister off is to tell me where Everspring is."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "I don't know where it is," you said. "You know I don't. I'm a guard. I carry plates."

"Of course you don't know." Vance smiled. "You're not the one I'm asking. You're the one I'm *using.* She'll talk to keep you from this. They always talk for the thing they love before they talk for themselves." He gestured at the trough. "Begin."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: There were two other men in the room. You understood, with a sick clarity, that if you refused, they would do it instead — and they would not count to ten, and they would not be gentle on the way down, and they would enjoy it.
So you crossed the floor on legs that did not feel like yours, and you knelt behind your sister, and you put your hands on her thin shoulders.
"Nessa," you breathed, too low for Vance. "Hold your breath when I press. Trust me. Hold it and I'll bring you up. I swear it. I swear it."
She nodded — one small, shaking nod — and that nod broke something in you that has not mended since.
"Where is Everspring?" Vance asked the empty air, because the question was never really for anyone in this room.
Silence.
"Down."

And you pushed your own sister's face into the ice-water and counted, and her body went rigid under your hands, and the water boiled with her thrashing, and you counted, ten, and pulled her up gasping and screaming and alive, and Vance said "Where is Everspring?" to no one, and the silence answered, and he said "Down," and you did it again.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Four times. Five. You lost the count of how many times you drowned the only blood you had left in the world a little and brought her back. Between them she sobbed your name, not in blame — never in blame, that was the unbearable part — but the way a child says it, asking the one person who is supposed to make things stop to please, please make it stop.
And you couldn't. You were the hands making it happen. That was the whole genius of it. Vance never touched her. He only watched your face, taking notes on exactly how much of you was left.
"Enough for the morning," he said at last, almost bored. "You're no good to me hollow. Go down. Beg. Come back when she's ready to be reasonable."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They let you wrap Nessa in your own coat before they dragged her back to her cell — small mercy, the only one you could win. Then you walked down the long stair to Elara's dark, your sleeves soaked to the elbow, the cold of the trough still living in your hands, and you did not know how you would say it.
She heard the water before you spoke. She always heard everything.
"You're wet," she said quietly, into the black. "All the way up your arms. What did they make you do."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And you told her. You knelt in the straw and you told her all of it — the trough, the ice, your own hands, the ten-counts, Nessa saying your name. Elara could not see any of it; she could only take it through your voice, which is its own particular cruelty, to be handed a horror you cannot look at and so can never quite put down.
You felt her go very still in her chains as you spoke. When you finished, she was quiet a long time.

"He's not torturing her," she said at last, and her voice was low and even and terrible with understanding. "He's torturing *you.* Through her, through me — we're all just instruments he's playing to find the one note that makes me open my mouth." A slow breath. "He's very good. I want you to hear me say that, so you stop thinking you can outfight him with your heart. You can't. Neither of us can. Not like this."
She leaned toward you, chains drawing tight.
"So we stop fighting like this. Starting now. While he thinks he's grinding us down, we're going to do the one thing he isn't watching for."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: "What thing," you said.

"We start *looking.*" You could hear the change in her — the rallied thing from last night, sharpening now into something with edges. "Six days. He keeps saying it to break us. I'm going to use it. Every time he sends you down here to break, you're going to bring me the room instead."

"Listen. When you walk these halls, you're a broken man begging — let him believe that, it's the best cover we'll ever have. But while you beg, you *count.* How many guards on the stair at the change of watch. What hour the torches are renewed and who carries the keys when they are. Where the cold air comes from — cold air means a way out, always. The rope on the upper beam, the drain in that stripped room, the door they never quite bolt because they think a chained woman and a heartbroken boy can't use it."

"Don't write anything. Don't plan anything yet. Just bring me the room, piece by piece, until I can walk it in my head in the dark." A pause, and something almost like warmth. "That's all today. Count the guards at the night change. Bring me that tomorrow. We have six days, and I am done spending them on grief."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You climbed the stair that night with your sleeves still damp and your sister's voice still in your ears — but for the first time, you climbed it counting. Two guards at the lower landing. One at the upper. The torch-bearer came at the turn of the third watch, keys on a ring at his left hip, and he yawned.
Small things. Nothing things. The beginning of everything.

Behind you in the dark, a princess who had wanted only to die was learning the shape of her prison by heart, one stolen detail at a time. Day two of six was over. Four more, and a plan with no pieces yet — only a soldier who had finally, quietly, decided to win.
— End of Chapter 12 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The days after the trough blurred into one long grey ache. Vance went on with his lever — the cane, the cold, the begging cycle — and it went on not working. Elara did not break for your sister's pain any more than for her own, and you, kneeling in the straw each evening, never once managed to truly beg. On the fourth day the king ran out of patience with the whole design.

Word came down that Nessa was being moved — not freed, but taken off the table, returned to an ordinary cell in the upper prison, fed, untouched. Vance's gamble had failed, and the king does not waste effort on a tool that has not worked.

It also meant the leash on your throat had gone slack. With your sister no longer under the knife, you spent those blurred nights doing the one thing Elara had asked: you brought her the room. The watch-change. The torch-bearer's keys. The cold draft that breathed up from a bricked-over drain behind the lower landing. Piece by piece, in the dark, the two of you had built a map. The escape was nearly ready.
And then they told you the execution was set for dawn — and that tonight, the king himself was coming down to ask her one last time.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: King Mordane came without fanfare. No herald, no guard of honor — just a tall, unhurried man in plain dark wool, a mage in grey at his shoulder, and four soldiers carrying something heavy under a cloth. He did not look like the monster who burned tax-late villages. He looked like a tired clerk. That was the most frightening thing about him.

"So this is her," he said, studying Elara in her chains as a man studies a horse he is deciding whether to buy. "Smaller than the stories." His eyes moved to you, the guard pressed against the wall. "And this is the one who's grown fond of her. Good. Stay. I want a witness who'll feel it."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The soldiers pulled the cloth away. Beneath it was a thing of black iron the king had ordered built for this night alone — a curved frame, like the spine of some great beast turned to metal, its arc rising to a cruel apex. A cradle, if a cradle were made to break the thing it held.

"Strip the blindfold," the king said. "I'm not Vance. I don't need her blind. I want her to watch her own king be reasonable." And to you: "You. Help them lay her over it. I'm told you have gentle hands. Use them. It will be the last gentleness she gets from anyone."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They forced you to do it — to lift her, to lay the small of her back against the iron apex and draw her wrists down to one side and her ankles to the other, until her whole body was bent backward over the curve, spine arched the wrong way, the way a body is never meant to bend. She made no sound as you did it. She only found your eyes, once, and held them, and you understood she was telling you: not your fault, keep your head, we are not done.

Then the soldiers hung weights from the cuffs at her wrists and ankles, and the arch deepened, and the skin across her breast — where Vance's lash had laid her open weeks ago and the wounds had only half-closed — stretched tight over the bend.
The half-healed lash-scars split. They opened down her front like seams giving way, and fresh blood ran in thin lines into the iron. She gasped — the first sound — through her teeth.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The king crouched beside her arched body, almost gentle, and produced from his coat a small clay jar. He worked the stopper loose and held it out — to you.

"Salt," he said, "and vinegar. An old remedy; it cleans a wound. And you have the gentlest hands in this room, so it should be yours that does it. Pour it into her. All of it. Into the open part." He watched your face. "Refuse, and I'll have the mage do it, and then I'll have you flogged on the same frame beside her. Pour it, and you both live to see the dawn. Choose quickly."

So your hands — the same hands that had loosened her cords that first night, that had wiped her tears under the stones — tipped the jar and poured salt and vinegar down into the torn lash-lines along her breast, and the scream that tore out of her then filled the whole dungeon and rang in the stone long after. She knew it was you. She always knew it was you. And still, through it, she did not blame you.
"Where is the Everspring, Elara?" the king asked, over her screaming, in exactly the tone one uses to ask the hour.
She wept, and shook on the iron, and the salt burned in her open front, and when she could finally make words they were not the words he wanted.

"You'll... you'll get nothing from me, clerk-king," she ground out. "You can split me down the middle. The spring dies with me. A man who wants to live forever is the one creature alive who must *never* be allowed to. I knew that at sixteen. I'll know it at the gallows."
Something flickered in Mordane's tired face — not anger. Almost respect. It was worse than anger.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The king did not rage at her defiance. He simply nodded, as if she had confirmed something, and pressed the clay jar back into your hands.

"Again," he said. "Deeper this time. And while you do it, Princess, hear my offer — because I make it only once." He crouched so his tired clerk's face was level with her upturned, straining one. "One word from you and there is no gallows at dawn. No rope. I will give you a life — a quiet room, a window, your sister Liora safe forever. All of it, for a place on a map. Speak, and you and this boy who loves you both walk out of here breathing. Stay silent, and I take the answer to the grave you'll be in by noon."
"Pour," he told you softly. "Let her think it over with the salt in her."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: So you poured again, and she screamed again, the salt and vinegar biting into the raw open lines down her breast the instant they touched her, her whole arched body wrenching against the chains. And again, when the king tilted his head. And again. There was no machine to it, no clever device — only an old jar, an old cruelty, and your own forced hands, over and over, while a king asked an unhurried question into her screaming.

"Where is the Everspring?" Touch. Scream. "One word and you live." Touch. Scream. "Liora, safe. A window. A life." Touch. Scream. He never lost his patience and he never raised his voice; he simply let the salt and your hands and the bend of the iron do the asking, hour after hour, certain that everyone breaks if you are only calm enough about it.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You stood there pouring agony into the woman you loved because the alternative was the mage's crueler hands and the frame beside her, and you learned that night exactly how much a man can hate himself and keep obeying. The hardest mercy was staying alive and useless, so you could be useful later.

And she would not break. Not for the salt, not for the offer of a life, not for Liora's name in the king's mouth. Somewhere in the third hour she stopped being able to form the word "no" and simply met the king's eyes, and then yours, and shook her ruined head — telling you, even now, with the same wordless thing she'd told you over the iron: not your fault. We are not done. And still, bent backward with her breast laid open and a kingdom's whole patience leaning on her, she would not give him the spring.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The king straightened, considering her the way a builder considers a wall that won't fall. "More weight," he said. "The big stones this time. You—" to you "—and you—" to the soldier at the wall "—hang them. On the wrists and the ankles both. I want her spine to learn what it's arguing with."

There was a heap of rough quarry-stones by the cradle's foot, each the size of a man's head. You and the soldier carried them two-handed and hung them from the cuffs, one to each limb, and with every stone the arch over the iron apex deepened — her body drawn further back over the curve than a body is built to go, the bones of her spine standing up under the stretched skin like a row of knuckles.
She made a sound with each one that you will hear for the rest of your life.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: When four stones hung from her, the king crouched and laid his open hand flat on her straining, upturned belly — almost tender — and was quiet a moment, feeling.

"There," he murmured. "Feel that? I can feel it through your skin — the place where your back is one stone from giving way. You're a finger's breadth from never standing again, Princess. From a chair and a blanket and someone to turn you for the rest of your life." He nodded toward the heap. "One more of those, on the count of three, and that's the woman you'll be — if you live at all. Or you say four words. *It is at—* and the name. Four words and the boy lifts the stones off you instead of onto you."

"One," he said. She wept and shook and stared at the ceiling. "Two." Her ruined breast heaved. And at *three* — when you stood frozen with the fifth stone in your arms, praying she'd break just so you wouldn't have to hang it — she dragged in a breath and said, in a thread of a voice: "Burn... first." So he did not have you hang it. He only looked at her, and something in his patience finally thinned.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: He stood, and set the sole of his boot against her bared, stretched throat.

Not a stamp — a press. Slow, measured, his weight easing down onto her windpipe while she lay pinned and arched and stoned-down and could not turn her head or lift a hand. Her mouth worked. No air came. Her face went red, then a dark dusky color, her eyes rolling to find yours, and you lunged half a step before the soldier's spear-haft caught you across the breast and held you back.

At the very edge of it — when she was a breath from going dark for good — the king lifted his boot, and let her claw back one screaming lungful, and asked into it, gently: "Where is the Everspring?" And when she only sobbed for air, he pressed down again. "The rope at dawn will be kinder than this," he told her, almost coaxing. "All you have to do to earn the kinder death is speak." She did not speak. Three times he took her to the edge of the dark and three times brought her back with nothing but a question, and three times she gave him her silence instead of her air.

It was the king who stopped first — but not to show mercy. He stepped back, took the empty jar from your shaking hands, and looked down at her bent and stoned-down and gasping with something almost like wonder. "Eleven years I've hunted that water," he said quietly, "and the last door is a girl on an iron frame who'd rather burn than open. I almost wish I'd had you in my army instead of across the field from it."

"But I am a patient man, and I have one night left." He turned to the soldiers. "Leave her on it. Exactly as she is — the stones stay, the bend stays. A whole night arched over that iron will say what three hours could not." He glanced at the dark mouth of the cell. "And I won't have her sleeping through it. Sleep is a mercy and she's earned none. Rig the basin."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They hung a wide copper basin from the beam above her, its bottom pricked through with a hundred pinholes, and filled it cold from the well — and made you be the one to haul it up and set it dripping. From then on, all night, the water came down on her in a slow ceaseless rain: onto her upturned face, into her nose, over the salt-raw wounds laid open down her breast, a fresh cold drop every breath or two, just often enough that her body could never once forget where it was and fall away into sleep.

"There," the king said, watching the first drops strike her. "By dawn she'll have been awake three days and bent in half for one, and either she'll give me the spring or she'll give the city a quiet hanging. Both serve." He drew his cloak straight. At the stair he paused, and without turning, almost to himself: "A pity. She was the only honest thing in this whole castle."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And then he was gone — and he did not let you stay. "You've served your purpose tonight, gentle hands," Vance said, taking you by the collar and steering you toward the steps while two fresh guards took the watch over the cradle. "Up. You'll have her back at dawn, what's left of her, for the walk to the rope."

You climbed the long stair with her blood and the salt-water drying on your sleeves and the steady tick of the dripping basin following you up out of the dark — drop, and drop, and drop — the sound of the woman you loved being kept awake and arched and freezing through her last night on earth, and you with a half-cut key and a vial of sleeping-draught in your boot and no way on this earth to reach her past two fresh guards and a castle full of the king's men.
Dawn was the execution. You had one night, no plan that survived contact with those two guards, and a drip counting it away. You did not sleep either.
— End of Chapter 13 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Dawn came grey and certain. They lifted her off the cradle at last — and three days without sleep and one whole night bent backward over iron had left her a thing that could barely be called standing. When they cut the stones loose and tried to straighten her, her spine would not unbend all at once; it came back in stages, each one tearing a sound out of her. They had to half-carry her up the long stair and out into the light she had not seen in weeks.

And the light was full of people. The whole city had come. They packed the square below the scaffold shoulder to shoulder, thousands of them, come to watch Valdere's butcher hang — and when she appeared, blinking and broken in the morning sun, the sound they made was not human. It was a wall of hate with ten thousand throats.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They stood her on the scaffold beneath the rope. King Mordane raised one hand and the square fell silent so fast you could hear the gulls.

"People of the capital," he called, unhurried, reasonable, the tired clerk made enormous by the crowd. "This woman led the army that burned your eastern fields. She has been asked, gently and ungently, for one thing that would buy her life — a single piece of knowledge she hoards out of spite. I'll ask her once more, where you can all hear it." He turned to her. "The Everspring, Elara. Speak, and you live. Stay silent, and these good people watch you drop. Choose, in front of them."
She lifted her head. It cost her everything to do it, but she lifted it, and she let the whole square see her ruined face, and when she spoke her cracked voice carried further than anyone expected.

"Your king," she said to the crowd, not to him, "wants to live forever. That is the secret he's tortured me three weeks to buy. Not safety. Not victory. *Forever.* Ask yourselves what a man like this does with a hundred years. A thousand." She swayed, caught herself. "I will die today so that he cannot. It is the best gift I will ever give your children. Pull the rope."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: It was the wrong thing for the king. A murmur went through the crowd — not sympathy, never that, but a flicker of unease, a question planted in ten thousand heads at once: *forever?* And the king heard it, and you watched him decide, in that instant, that he could not afford to let the rope make a martyr of her with that word hanging in the air.

"No," he said, and lowered his hand. "No — a quick drop is too clean for what she's earned. The traitor doesn't hang today." He smiled at the crowd, recovering, turning it. "Today she answers to *you.*"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They had a pillory waiting at the edge of the scaffold — a heavy oak frame, the kind that clamps a neck and two wrists and bends a body forward to stand stooped and helpless for all to see. They locked her into it there above the square.

"Three weeks my questioners had her," the king called, "and got nothing. Perhaps the people she wronged will do better. She stands here until dusk. You may give her the justice you're owed — all of you, as you please." A pause, and then the one rule, not for mercy but for ownership: "Only she does not die. She is mine to hang, when I choose. Leave her breathing for me."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And he set you, and a line of guards, around the foot of the pillory — not to protect her. To protect his property. Your orders, from Vance's own mouth: keep the mob from killing her. Let them do everything short of it. Stand here, gentle hands, and make sure they don't finish what the king wants to finish himself.
So you stood, in the line, between the woman you loved and the city that wanted her dead, and the only thing your sword was permitted to do was keep her alive for a worse death.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They came in a flood. The first rotten fruit struck her face before the king was off the scaffold; then it was filth from the gutters, dung, fish-heads, spit — a whole city emptying its hate onto a woman who could not raise a hand to wipe her own eyes. They jeered the word she'd given them and threw harder for it. An old man got close and struck her across the face again and again with a switch until a guard bored him and shoved him back into the press.

Some of them, you understood, had earned this. You could see it on the ones who didn't shout — the woman who simply stood at the rail and wept while she threw, the man who said a name, a son's name, with every stone. Elara had burned their fields. The grief in that square was real. That was the worst of it: it was not all monsters hurting her. It was the wronged, and she had wronged them, and there is no clean place to stand in that.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: By midday they had shorn her hair off — a butcher's wife climbed up with shears to a great roar and hacked it away in fistfuls, and the long dark hair you used to ease back from her face when she ate fell into the muck of the scaffold and was trampled. They pelted her bared scalp. The sun came round and beat on the bent back of her neck where the pillory held her. A thrown cobble caught her brow and opened it and the blood ran down into her eyes and mixed with the filth and she could not wipe it, and still — every hour, when she could find the air — she lifted her clamped head as far as the oak would let her and faced them, and would not weep for them, and would not beg.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Twice, men threw stones meant to kill — heavy, head-high, the kind that ends a life. Both times you moved without deciding to: once your shield took it, once you knocked the arm. You told yourself it was the king's order, keep her breathing, only the order. But she felt it. Bent and blind with blood, she knew which guard kept stepping between her and the killing stones, and once, when you were near enough, she breathed two words through her split lips, under the roar, just for you: "Not yet." Telling *you* to hold. To stay alive and useless a little longer. To not throw it all away saving her in front of ten thousand witnesses.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: It went on until the light went amber and the crowd's arm finally tired, the way even hatred tires. By dusk the square was emptying, the people drifting home to their suppers as if they had not spent a day stoning a bound woman, and what was left in the pillory barely moved.

Vance came to unlock her. "Still breathing," he noted, almost disappointed, tilting her ruined face up by the chin. "The king will be pleased. You're a stubborn thing." He let her head drop. "He hasn't set a new day for the rope. He says you'll hang when you break, and not before. Could be tomorrow. Could be a long, long time."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They carried her back down into the dark, and it was you who was made to wash the filth and the blood from her in the cell, your hands shaking, her shorn head bare under your palms, neither of you saying what you both now knew: that there was no execution date left to escape *before* — only an open, bottomless stretch of days in which the king would hurt her until she died of it, on no schedule but his patience.
Which meant the clock you'd been racing was gone. And a man with no deadline either runs out of hope — or stops waiting for the perfect night, and starts making one.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She slept at last, that night — the dead, dropped sleep of a body that has nothing left — with her bare head in your lap and your back to the cell door, and you sat awake over her counting guards in your mind, and watch-changes, and the cold breath of the bricked drain, turning the half-cut key over and over in your fingers.
No deadline. No perfect night. Just a princess who had told a whole city the truth and lived, and a guard who had finally, fully run out of reasons to wait.
— End of Chapter 14 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The king had no calendar to keep now, and that made him worse, not better. A man in a hurry makes mistakes; a man with forever makes plans. For days he let her rot in the dark and turned the problem over, and then he found a new road — and it was the oldest one, dressed up crueler. He went back to your sister.

"Vance's little game failed because it was hidden," the king said, the morning they hauled you both out into the open. "Pain behind a door is a rumor. Pain in the sun is a lever. We'll do it where the princess can't look away — and where the city can watch her choose."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They had built it in the open ground below the walls: a tall timber A-frame, and a single great pulley-wheel at its peak with one rope run over it, a noosed cuff at each end. A crowd was already gathering at the rope-lines the guards strung up, the same city that had stoned her, come to see what new thing the king had made.

And they made *you* rig it. Vance put the cords in your hands and stood over you while you tied your own sister's wrists behind her back, and then the princess's, and threaded the rope over the wheel, and learned — knot by knot, with your own fingers — exactly how the cruelty worked.
Vance walked the crowd through it like a showman, delighted to be useful again.

"Simple, and fair," he called. "The girl on this side is weak — a slip of a thing, the traitor-guard's sister, no concern of yours. The princess on that side is strong. So we let the strong one carry the weak one." He gestured to the iron. "We hang the weights on Her Highness. As long as she holds them — arms up, on her feet — the rope stays taut and the girl stands easy. The moment the princess sags, the rope runs, and the girl is hauled up off the earth by her bound arms until her shoulders leave their sockets. The princess decides, with her own strength, whether the child is hurt. Isn't that just?"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Then they loaded her.

They hung iron from the cuffs at her wrists — bar after bar of it, drawing her arms up and back and out, until even she, who had borne the cradle and the stones and the salt, made a low animal sound she could not stop. The weight was past what a strong man could hold, let alone a woman three days starved and a night bent over iron. Her arms drew taut as ship's rope, the muscle standing out, and within minutes the skin of her shoulders and forearms went a deep, furious red, then darker, the blood trapped and pounding where the cords bit.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And Nessa, on the other end, was weak — too weak to hold herself steady. Every little while her exhausted legs gave a fraction and her weight pulled down on her side of the rope, and the whole system answered: the pull ran over the wheel and hauled the princess up onto the points of her toes, the iron swinging, her shoulders screaming, until she fought her heels back to the ground and steadied them both.

"Hold still, Nessa," Elara breathed across the gap between them, her voice somehow gentle through her teeth. "Don't fight it, sweetheart. Just stand. I have you. I have you. Stand, and let me hold us both." And your sister wept and tried to stand, and could not always manage it, and every time she failed the princess paid for it in her arms — and never once let the rope drop her.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The king watched from his chair and was not satisfied. Holding is not breaking. After an hour of it he turned, almost lazily, to the man at his shoulder.

"Vance. You wanted another chance to be useful. Here it is." He nodded at the strung-up princess. "She's standing too well. Give her a reason to fall — and let's see if she'll let the girl drop to spare her own skin. Whip her."

Something lit in Vance's face that was worse than cruelty — it was *gratitude.* He had failed the king for weeks; here, at last, before the whole court and city, was his road back into favor, and it ran across the princess's body. He took up the whip and shook it loose and walked to where she hung.
"You've cost me a great deal, Highness," he said quietly, only to her. "Let me return some of it."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The first lash fell across her breast — over the half-healed scars his own whip had carved there weeks ago, over the lines the salt had reopened — and it laid them bare again in a spray of red. But the true cruelty was not the lash. It was what the lash demanded.

Because if she flinched from it — if her body did what a whipped body must, and recoiled, and her arms dropped even a hand's breadth — the rope would run and Nessa would be torn off the earth. So she could not flinch. She had to take each stroke standing dead still, balanced on her ruined feet, her arms locked up under their iron, absorbing the whip into a body that was forbidden to move. Vance struck, and she held. He struck again, and she held, a sound tearing out of her throat that her body was not allowed to follow.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: He found his rhythm and the king leaned forward and the crowd went quiet, and Vance laid the whip across her front again and again, proving himself stroke by stroke, and each one she met without falling. Her breast ran red. Her arms shook under the iron. Her toes scrabbled and caught and held. And between the lashes, when she could find a thread of air, she did not curse Vance and she did not beg the king — she spoke to your sister.
"Almost done, Nessa. You're doing so well. Keep standing. Don't watch me — watch your brother, there in the line, watch his face, he's going to get you home. Just stand, love. Just a little more."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And you stood in the guard-line where she'd told the girl to look, and you watched the woman you loved be flayed across the breast for the crime of refusing to let your sister fall, and you understood that you were watching the bravest thing you would ever see, and that you had tied the knots that made it possible.

Once — once — Nessa's legs went entirely, all the way, and the rope ran fast and snatched Elara up and the iron swung wild and for one heartbeat the princess was off the ground entirely, hung from her own torn shoulders with the whole weight on her, screaming at last, a real scream — and then she got a toe down, and dragged it back, and steadied, and gasped to your sister, "It's all right. It's all right. I've got you. Stand." She would have died on that rope before she let it drop the girl. Everyone in the square could see it. Even the king.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: It was Vance's arm that tired first. He had whipped her past the count anyone was keeping, and she had not fallen, and she had not given the king his spring, and she had not let Nessa touch the air — and slowly the thing he'd meant as his triumph curdled, because a torturer who cannot break his victim has not proven himself strong. He has proven her unbreakable in front of everyone watching.

The king saw it too, and his jaw tightened, and he rose and ended it — not from mercy, but because every further stroke only made the princess larger and his man smaller. "Enough. Take them down." And under the cut of his voice, just audible: "...she should have broken. Why won't she break."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: They lowered the iron and unstrung them both. Nessa, untorn, unsocketed, alive — saved entire by a woman who had been whipped raw rather than drop her an inch — collapsed into your arms, and Elara folded down into the dirt with her arms hanging wrong and her breast a ruin, conscious only enough to turn her shorn head toward the two of you and see, with something like peace, that the girl was whole.
"Told you," she whispered, to no one, to all of you. "I had her."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: That night you sat between them in the dark — your sister, returned to her cell with a guard you'd bribed to look away an hour; the princess, laid out and barely breathing in hers — and something in you finished changing.

There was no deadline to beat. There was no perfect night coming. There was only a woman who would let herself be destroyed before she let his cruelty win, and a man who had finally seen, past all his fear, that the only unforgivable thing left was to make her keep doing it alone.
You did not turn the half-cut key over in your fingers that night. You finished cutting it.
— End of Chapter 15 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: It took two days to be ready. Two days of carrying her water and her bread and saying nothing with your mouth and everything with your hands, while underneath you cut and filed and waited and stole what the run would need — a coil of rope, a flat-bottomed skiff dragged into the reeds below the river outflow, a bundle of dry clothes, and the small blue vial that had ridden in your boot since the day you made it.

And on the third night, the castle gave you your window. The king threw a feast in the great hall — for Vance. To celebrate his man's return to favor, the breaking of the princess's public spirit that wasn't a breaking at all. The garrison drank his health till the torches guttered. And out past the walls, a storm came walking up the river, throwing the first fat drops against the stone, swelling the black water, drowning the night in noise.
Everything you had waited for had come at once. You stopped waiting.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You carried the dungeon-watch their wine yourself — gentle hands, trusted hands, no one looked twice — and you had thumbed the blue vial empty into the jug on the stair. The two men on the lower landing drank to Vance and to the king and to the hanging that would surely come now, and within the quarter-hour the first was snoring against the wall and the second slid down beside him with the cup still in his fist.

The third-watch torch-bearer came round at his hour, yawning, the key-ring at his hip, and you met him with a smile and a last cup, and when he folded you eased him down quiet and lifted the ring from his belt. Two doors' worth of iron, warm from his body. The upper levels, and the lower. Nessa, and Elara.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You went down to her first. You could not have done it the other way; some compass in you pointed there and would not be argued with.

The deepest cell was black and close and full of the sound of the storm coming down through the stone from far above, and of her breathing — shallow, careful, the breathing of a body learning how to exist around its own wounds. You crossed to the bars and your hand was shaking so badly the finished key chattered against the lock before it found the slot, and turned, and the door you had locked behind you a hundred times swung open for you for the first time.

She heard the wrong sound — a door opening when no door should — and her ruined body flinched back into the straw, bracing for whatever new thing they'd built, and her cracked voice came out of the dark trying to be steady and not managing it.
"...Whatever it is," she whispered, "do it and let me sleep. I'll still say no. I'll always say—"

"Elara." You were on your knees in front of her before you knew you'd moved. "It's me. It's only me. There's no one else. Listen to me — listen — the watch is down. The whole watch. The storm's covering us and the feast has the rest of them drunk and there is a boat in the reeds below the river drain. Do you understand what I'm telling you?"

She went very still. In the dark you felt rather than saw her lift her shorn head, felt the whole of her come awake at once the way she had on the night her will came back, and when she spoke it was barely a thread.
"Say it again," she breathed. "Say it plainly. I've dreamed it too many times and woken up still here. Tell me plainly so I know it's you and not my own mind being cruel."

"Tonight," you said, and you took her poor cold face in both your hands. "Tonight I take you out of here. Both of you. We are not waiting for a kinder day, because there isn't one coming — there's only us, and a hole in the wall, and a river. Tonight you stop being theirs. I swear it on every cruelty they made me do to you. I'm taking you home."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She made a sound then that was not a sob and was not a laugh and was somehow both — the sound of a person who has held a wall up for so long that the wall coming down feels like falling. And she pressed her wet face hard into your palm, into the same hand that had loosened her cords on the first night and poured the salt into her wounds on the worst one, and she did not flinch from it, and that — that she would still turn toward your hand after everything it had been made to do — undid you completely.
"All right," she whispered against your skin. "All right. I believe you. God help me, I believe you. Get these off me and take me out of the dark."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You found the cuffs by touch. Her wrists were a horror — raw and crusted and swollen from the weights, the cords sunk into the flesh — and you worked the iron loose as gently as your shaking hands allowed, and still each one tore a hiss out of her, and each hiss tore something out of you.

When the last of it fell away her arms came free and dropped uselessly into her lap, the shoulders wrenched too far to lift, and she looked down at them in the faint storm-light leaking from above and gave a small broken laugh. "They don't work," she said, almost wondering. "I've nothing left to even hold onto you with. After all this, you'll have to carry me out like luggage."
"Then I'll carry you," you said. "You walked in here on your own feet to save your sister. You don't have to walk out. Let me be the strong one for one night. Let me carry you."

For a moment she didn't answer. Then, in the dark, she leaned her forehead against yours — the only part of her that still obeyed her — and stayed there, breathing you in, and when she spoke her voice had something in it he had never once heard from her in all these weeks: not defiance, not despair, but the simple, terrified tenderness of someone letting themselves want a thing again.

"Do you know," she murmured, "that you are the only gentle thing that has happened to me since the snow? They sent me a guard to keep me alive so they could destroy me, and instead the guard is the reason there was anything left in me worth destroying. I held on for a thousand reasons and most of them were lies I told myself. The last one wasn't." Her brow pressed harder to his. "The last one was you."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And then, because there was a storm above and a boat below and a whole short life of waited-for things pressing on the one moment they finally had — you closed the last inch of the dark between you and you kissed her.

Gently, so gently, mindful of her split lip and her ruined mouth, a kiss that asked nothing and promised everything, weeks of forbidden meals and stolen mercies and unsaid words all pouring into it at once. She could not raise her arms to hold you, so she gave you the only thing her body would still surrender — she kissed you back, fierce and trembling and alive, a princess and a guard tasting the first free thing either of them had had in a very long time, in the bottom of the deepest cell in the kingdom, while the rain came down.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: When you parted she was crying and smiling at once, and so, you realized, were you.
"That," she whispered shakily, "was a very stupid thing to do with the watch only drugged and not dead. Do it once more anyway. Quickly. In case the river takes us and that was my only chance at it."

So you did. And then you made yourself stop, because love would not get her over the wall and time would, and you wiped her face with your sleeve and she let you, and you slid your arms beneath her — one behind her wrecked shoulders, one beneath her knees — and you lifted her up out of the straw she had bled into for a month.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She weighed almost nothing. That was its own grief — how light they had made her, how much of her they had taken — but she settled against your breast as if she had been made to fit there, and turned her shorn head into the side of your neck, and let out a long, shuddering breath that seemed to carry a month of the dark out with it.

"I have you," you said into her hair — the words she had spent her last strength saying to your sister on the rope, given back to her now. "Do you hear me, Elara? I have you. The dark doesn't. Not anymore."

"I hear you," she whispered. "Then go. Get your sister. And get us all to that river." A breath, and then, so quiet you almost missed it under the rain: "...I'm not finished with you, guardsman. When we're free, you and I are going to have a very long conversation about the rest of our lives."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You carried her out of the open cell and into the black throat of the dungeon stair, her heartbeat against your ribs, the storm roaring somewhere above, the drugged watch sprawled and snoring and the whole sleeping castle between you and the river.

Two doors of iron, warm in your pocket. A sister waiting one floor up. A loosened drain that breathed the outside world. And in your arms, at last, the woman you had been told to keep alive — alive, and free of her chains, and looking up at you in the dark as if you were the morning.

It was not over. The hardest part was still ahead, and Vance was still drinking his own health one hall away. But for the length of that first staircase, with her held against your heart, you let yourself believe it could be done.
— End of Chapter 16 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The upper cells were not like the deep dungeon. Here the stone was drier, the torches farther apart, and the cold came not from the earth but from the river — you could hear it now, swollen and furious beyond the wall, the storm feeding it.

You set Elara down at the turn of the stair, in the deepest shadow, and crouched so your faces were level. "Nessa is up there," you breathed. "Last cell, end of the gallery. There's a guard on the gallery — there's always a guard. I need you to stay here. You can barely stand."
She gripped your sleeve with the hand that still worked.
"I have spent two years learning to be useful while in chains," she whispered. "Do not make me start being useless the night I am out of them."
Her split lip pulled when she smiled. "You will need both hands for your sister. Let me be the thing the guard is looking at instead."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You hated that she was right. A man carrying a key-ring and a chisel up a guarded gallery has nowhere to put his eyes that doesn't look like guilt. But a man can do anything in a corridor where the guard is staring the other way.
"If it goes wrong," you said, "you scream the wall down and you run for the drain. You don't come back for me."
"Liar," she said gently. "You would never obey that order either." And she let go of your sleeve.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The gallery guard was a thick-necked man named Holt, and he was bored, and boredom is the torturer's best friend and the jailer's worst. He had his back to the cells and his face to a slit window, watching the rain come sideways.

Elara went first — not creeping, but walking, the way only the highborn can walk even barefoot and ruined, as if the floor were honored to have her. She let her shackle-chain drag once on the stone so it sang.
Holt turned with his hand on his cudgel and then forgot the cudgel entirely.

"You are the new watch?" she said, and her voice did something — went low and warm and amused, a voice from a banquet and not a cell. "They send a man like you to guard a corridor of empty rooms. What a waste of a wide pair of shoulders."
She came closer than a prisoner should dare, into the torchlight, chin up. "Tell me your name, watchman. I would like one kind face to remember from this place."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: It should not have worked. Holt had been told the princess was a viper, a witch, a liar — and every word was true, and none of it mattered, because she had turned the full and practiced charm of a court on a lonely man on a long night, and that is not seduction so much as a key cut for a particular lock.
He stepped toward her. He turned, fully, away from the cells. He started to say his name.
Behind him, you came up the gallery on the balls of your bare feet with the key-ring strangled in your fist so it could not ring.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Nessa's cell was the last. Through the bars you saw her — nineteen and grey-faced and awake, always awake now, her wrists in a short wall-chain that let her sit but not lie down. She saw you and her whole body jerked toward the bars and you put one finger to your lips so hard it hurt.
She understood. She had always been the clever one. She went still and silent and only her eyes screamed.
The cell lock took the second key. It opened like a held breath let go.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The wrist-chain was the problem. It was not locked to her — it was riveted to a ring sunk in the wall, an old job, the iron grown into the mortar, and no key on the ring would touch it. This was the digging you had dreaded.

You wedged the chisel where the wall-ring met the stone and you began to work it, a finger's width at a time, packing your cloak around the head to swallow the sound. The mortar was old. It came away in wet grey crumbs. But it came slowly, and every scrape was a noise in a quiet castle.
Down the gallery, Holt laughed at something the princess said. Good. Laughter is loud.

Elara kept him. You could hear it — the murmur, the low laugh, the question that made him answer, the answer that made him lean in. She walked him in a slow half-circle without ever seeming to move him at all, until his back was to the whole length of the gallery and the storm covered the rest.
Once she laughed, bright and delighted, at nothing, exactly when your chisel shrieked on stone.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The mortar gave. The ring tilted, ground, and tore loose from the wall with a gout of grit, and Nessa's chain dropped slack into your hands. You caught it before it could hit the floor and bunched it against your breast, both of you frozen, listening.
Rain. River. A bored man laughing at a princess.

You pulled Nessa up. She weighed nothing. She pressed her face into your neck and shook, all of it coming out silent, and you held the back of her head the way you had when she was small and the world was only as large as one bad night.
"Sister," you breathed into her hair. "I have you. We're going. Not a sound, not a stumble. You walk where I walk."

She nodded against you. Then she lifted her head and looked past you at the woman down the gallery still holding a guard in the palm of her voice, and something passed over Nessa's ruined face — not jealousy. Recognition. "That's her," she mouthed. "That's the one you talk to in your sleep."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You did not have time to deny it and you would not have managed it anyway. You bundled Nessa's chain up short so it could not drag, put her behind you, and started back down the gallery the way you'd come.

Now the only trouble left in the corridor was Holt — and a man cannot stare at a princess forever, not when his relief is due and his bladder is full and some animal part of him has begun to wonder why the empty cells smell of fresh-broken mortar.

Elara felt the moment turning before you did. She always did. "Walk me to the window," she told Holt, suddenly, gaily, taking one more step — putting her own body squarely between the guard's eyes and the three of you slipping behind him toward the stair. "I want to see the storm before they hang me. Surely a man like you won't deny a dying woman the rain."
Holt, helpless, walked her to the window. And the gallery behind him emptied of everyone he had been charged to keep.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You reached the stairhead with Nessa pressed to your back. Elara, at the window, let the guard have one last moment of his strange enchanted night — and then, between one gust and the next, she simply was not there. She drifted back from him, into the dark of the turn, and your hand found her wrist and drew her down the steps with you.
Holt blinked at the empty window for a long while before he understood that the most beautiful thing that had ever happened to him had been a thief.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Three of you now, on the cold lower stair: a broken princess, a starved sister, and a guard who had betrayed everything he was sworn to. Above you, an empty gallery. Below you, a drain that breathed the river. Between, a sleeping castle and one drunk captain.
Nessa's hand was in your left. Elara's was in your right. For one heartbeat you were a bridge between the two people you would die for, and both of them were on the same side of the wall at last.
"The drain," Elara whispered. "Take us to the wall that breathes."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You went down toward the river-sound, toward the loosened stones and the staged skiff and the storm that would either drown you or hide you. Behind and above, the castle slept on, sure of its locks.
