It did not yet know that its cruelest cell was empty, and its best leash was cut, and the princess it meant to hang was walking out through its own foundations on the arm of its own guard.
It would know soon. Vance would wake. But not yet. Not for one more flight of stairs.
— End of Chapter 17 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You took them down through the foundations the way you had walked it a hundred times in your head — the cold lower passage where the drain breathed, the loosened stones you had worked over a dozen night-watches, the dark that smelled of river instead of iron.

Elara could not climb and Nessa could barely walk, so you went slow, a hand on each of them. You were perhaps thirty paces from the breathing stones when, far above and behind you, the castle stopped sleeping.
It began as one bell. Then every bell.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Vance had not gone to bed. A captain restored to favor does not sleep on the night of his triumph — and somewhere between the feast and his quarters he had gone down to look at the woman who had cost him everything and given it back.
He found the lower landing strewn with snoring men, a cell standing open and empty, chains lying cut on the straw, still warm, and the second key gone from the torch-bearer's ring.

Vance was many cruel things but never a fool. He understood the whole of it in a single breath — the guard, the looks, the weak draught, the princess who would not break — and he threw back his head and roared the castle awake.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The order went out in his voice, carrying down the stairwells like cold water: "The traitor has the enemy princess and his own sister! Every gate, every wall! Gold to whoever brings her back breathing — and the guard's head I want myself!"

Hundreds of boots, all at once, in every corridor of the keep. You reached the breathing stones and put your shoulder to the mortar you had patiently murdered over a month of stolen nights. The old, forgotten sally-port gave way into a gust of wet wind and the open, storm-black night.

You poured all three of you out onto the slick rock above the river. The staged skiff waited in the reeds, pale in the dark — not forty paces downstream. Forty paces between you and the black water that would carry you free.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You never got to take them.

Torches spilled out of the broken wall behind you — and more came around the foot of the tower ahead, a line of them fanning across the rock. Vance had not only chased; he had sent men around the outside. In a dozen heartbeats you went from almost-free to surrounded: the three of you backed against the roaring river, soldiers closing from both sides.

You drew the short guard's blade at your hip — one sword, against a tightening ring of spears, a wounded princess at your back and your sister clinging to your arm. It was not a fight. It was the few seconds before an ending.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And then Elara stepped past you.

She stepped past you into the torchlight and the rain — and it struck you like a blow that it was the first time in two years you had seen her stand with nothing on her wrists. No chains. No shackles. No rope. Just a princess on her own two feet under an open sky.

She did not reach for your sword. She did not reach for a fallen spear. She let her empty hands hang loose at her sides, and slowly, deliberately, she rolled the wreck of her shoulders back and lifted her chin, and you realized you were about to see something the king's dungeon had never once let out of her.

"Save your sister." She did not look back at you; her eyes were already moving over the soldiers, counting, measuring. "That is the only order I have ever given you that I need you to obey. Get Nessa to the high country. I will hold them here."
"Elara—" Your voice broke on it.

"Before I was a prisoner, before I was ever a princess of war," she said, very quietly, "I was a child in the training courts of my mother's house, and they taught me the open-hand forms before they ever let me hold a blade. Two years of iron did not take that out of me. Let these men learn what my homeland teaches its daughters."

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She bent for one quick moment and tore the trailing, sodden hem of her ruined skirt, knotting the wet fabric short and tight against her thigh so it could not foul her legs — a fighter clearing her own footwork, nothing more. Then she set her bare feet on the wet stone, sank her weight low, and drew her hands up before her in a guard you had never seen: one palm open and forward, one drawn back at the hip, elbows soft, breathing slow.

From somewhere far inside her, under the brand and the lash-scars and the wrenched shoulders, an old voice surfaced — her first master's, from a sunlit courtyard a lifetime and a war away. Stillness first, the voice said. Let them bring you the fight. You do not have to be stronger than ten men. You have to be exactly where they are not.
She breathed out. She waited.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The first soldier came fast and clumsy, spear leveled at her belly. She did not back away from it — she stepped in, off the line, turning her hips, and let his own lunge carry him past her; her forward palm snapped up under his jaw with the whole turn of her body behind it, and his head went back and his feet went out and he hit the rock and did not rise.
One, she thought. The form is still in me. Thank the old gods, it is still in me.

Her split lip was bleeding again and she had not even felt the strike land. It was almost peaceful. For the first time in two years her body was hers, doing the thing it had been shaped to do before the world ever taught it pain.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The second and third came together, wiser, spreading to take her from two sides. She flowed between them like water finding the low ground — a low sweeping kick that took the left man's knee out from under him, a pivot, an elbow turned into the right man's ribs, a twist of his own wrist that sent his spear clattering into the dark. Down. Down.

But it cost her, and you saw it cost her. When she snapped that kick high, the strappado-wrenched shoulders screamed and her arm dropped a fraction too slow; when she twisted, the half-healed lash-wounds across her breast split open afresh under the rain, and a thin dark line bled through the ruined cloth. The torn skirt came loose mid-pivot and tangled her ankle — she ripped it free with a snarl without ever breaking the form.
Each strike was a debt her starved, tortured body could not really pay. She paid it anyway, and smiled through it, because every soldier on the ground was one more second of your sister's life.

"RUN!" she screamed — not turning, her voice cracking clean in half on the word, tears and rain streaming down a face that was still, impossibly, fighting. "For the love of everything that is left — TAKE HER AND RUN!"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Every part of you that had loosened her cords and wiped her tears and carried her up that long dark stair was screaming to stay and die at her side. You did not take a step back. You took a step toward her.
"I'm not leaving you," you said, and you barely knew you'd said it. "I came down into this place to get you out. I am not walking out of it without you—"

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And then Nessa — small, starved, terrified Nessa — seized your sword-arm with both her hands and hauled you backward with all the weight she had left in her body.
"She's GIVING us this!" your sister sobbed against your shoulder. "Don't you dare waste it. Don't you dare make her do this for nothing — RUN, brother, run, RUN!"

So you turned away. It was the hardest thing you have ever done, and you will carry it the rest of your life: you turned your back on the princess fighting alone in the rain, and you ran, your sister's hand crushed in yours, up the dark track toward the high country.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Behind you the torchlight thickened. A fresh wave of soldiers was pouring out of the broken wall now, more and more of them flooding onto the narrow shelf of rock, and through the rain your last backward glimpse was of a single small figure at the center of it all — still standing, still moving, still turning men away with nothing but her hands and her feet and her unbreakable, unbroken will.
Then the track bent, and the rocks rose between you, and she was gone from your sight — but not, you swore into the storm, gone for good.
— End of Chapter 18 —

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You ran until the river was a silver thread far below and the castle a distant clutch of torches, until your lungs were fire and your sister's legs were failing. You ran until the land tilted up hard and the black mountains rose enormous ahead, and only when Nessa could not take another step did you stop, on a high cold shoulder of stone, and turn, and look back the way you had come.
Far, far below, on that little shelf of rock above the water, you could still see her. And your heart stopped.
She was not holding three soldiers now. She was holding ten.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: A single figure ringed in torchlight, with the black river at her back and ten armed men in a closing arc before her — and still she fought them bare-handed, the way her mother's house had taught her in a courtyard a war and a lifetime away.

Even at that terrible distance you could read the forms: the way she never met a spear straight but turned it, slid past it, used the man's own weight against him; the way she struck once, hard, exactly where he was open, and was already moving before he fell. A palm to a throat. A heel to the back of a knee. A turn that sent two of them stumbling into each other in the dark.
Hold your center, the old voice said inside her, calm as a sunlit morning. Ten men cannot all reach you at once. Make them take turns. Make each one pay.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You did not know — you could not have known — what it was costing her to make it look like that.

Inside the body that moved so beautifully, everything was failing at once. Her starved muscles burned through the last of what little they had left. The brand below her collarbone was a coal under her skin. The lash-wounds across her breast had torn fully open and the rain ran pink down the front of her ruined dress. Her wrenched shoulders shrieked with every block. And her bare feet and shins, cut to ribbons on the wet rock, left dark prints with every step she took.
One more, she told herself, each time another man came in. One breath. One form. One more, and they are one breath farther from the mountain. Hold. Just hold.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: The torn skirt fought her as hard as the soldiers did. The wet, ragged cloth wound around her knees, snatched at her kicks, threatened her balance every time she pivoted, and twice she had to tear it free one-handed in the middle of the fight, snarling, refusing to let a scrap of cloth do what ten men could not.

She did not let it. She knotted it tighter, set her bleeding feet wider, and kept her center low, and went on — because somewhere on a dark mountain two people she had decided to save were still climbing, and a princess of her blood does not stop while there is one more breath of distance left to buy.
This is what I am for, she thought, almost wondering at it through the haze of pain. Not the spring. Not the throne. This. Standing between the ones I love and the dark. Let it be this.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: And then, at last, it left her.

It was not one blow that did it. It was two years come due all at once — the cradle, the press, the brand, the strappado, the days without food or water or sleep — and a body, however brave, however trained, however royal, can only be spent so far before there is simply nothing left to draw on.

Her legs, cut and bleeding and shaking, finally would not answer her. A high block came a heartbeat too slow. A pivot did not turn. The beautiful, flowing forms stuttered and broke, and for the first time the ring of men was faster than she was.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: A guard caught her from behind, both her wrists locked in his fists.

Even then — even spent, even finished — she did not simply give up. She dropped her weight, turned inside his grip the way the forms had taught her, tore one hand free and drove her elbow back into him so hard he folded and let go.
But it was the last of her. There was nothing after it. And the others saw it too.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Four of them closed on her at once. Then five. They caught her arms, her shoulders, bore her down by sheer weight of bodies, pinning the warrior under a press of armored men who would not have dared come within reach of her a minute before.

And still — God, still — she fought them. Weakened, swaying, half-blind with exhaustion and pain, she strained against their hands, twisting, refusing to go still, because going still was a thing she did not know how to do.
From your mountain you watched it and you could not breathe. Nessa pressed her face into your side so she would not have to see.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: She knew. Some clear, calm part of her, even now, knew exactly how this ended — a whole army against one starved, chained-and-unchained princess on a strip of wet rock, and only one way for the arithmetic to come out. There was no winning this. There never had been.

She fought anyway. With every scrap of spirit left in her, with the last forms her body could still remember, she fought as though she did not know the ending at all — because the fight was never about winning. It was about the seconds, and every second was a step you and Nessa climbed farther into the dark mountains and out of their reach.

And then, between one breath and the next, the darkness simply rose up and swallowed her sight. Her body — a princess's body, born to strength, raised to it, made for it — had nothing left to give; the months of the cradle and the press and the brand and the starving had finally spent the very last of her. Her knees buckled. The torchlight smeared and went out. She folded down onto the wet stone, unconscious before she landed.

It was done, from her side. She had held them long enough. The two people she loved were safe, far up a black mountain where no soldier would follow tonight — and in the last flickering instant before everything went dark, knowing that, she smiled. And then she fainted.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Then, through the thinning rain, you saw him come.
Vance. Unhurried now. Walking out into the torchlight with chains gathered in his two hands, taking his time, savoring it — the one prize the whole night had failed to deny him.

They held her limp, senseless body still while he shackled her. Wrists first. Then the iron collar. Then the long, heavy chain — locking back onto her, link by link, every single iron thing she had stood up under the open sky to be free of, fastened now onto a woman too far gone to even feel it close.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: There was no walking her back. She was long past that.

Two soldiers took her under the arms and dragged her limp between them, her cut bare feet trailing over the wet rock, her shorn head hanging loose. The princess who had held ten armed men at bay an hour before was carried off senseless, back toward the gate, back into the castle she had bled and fought and spent the very last of herself to escape.
The dark she had begged you never to let take her was taking her back, and there was not one thing on this earth you could do about it from a mountain a thousand feet above.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: You stood on that high shoulder of stone and watched them carry the unconscious shape of her down off the rock, and you could not breathe, and you could not move, and you could not look away.

You will see it behind your eyes every night for the rest of your life: her head hanging, her arms loose, the chains swinging at her wrists, the torchlight swallowing her, the dark closing over her again.

Beside you, Nessa pressed her face into your side and wept, and you held her, and neither of you said a word, because there were no words left in the world for what you had just watched her do for you.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: But you held on to one thing in that moment, and you will hold on to it for the rest of your days.

The last thing she did, up there in the thick of ten men, before the darkness rose and took her — you were far too distant to have truly seen it, and you knew it anyway, the way you always somehow knew her: she had smiled.

She had spent every last drop of herself and she had won the only victory she had ever wanted — yours — and knowing the two of you stood free and uncaught on a far black mountain, she had let go and gone down into the dark glad. It was the face of a woman who had lost everything and regretted nothing.

nodes.speaker: narrator
lines: Then they hauled her through the gate, and the dark of the castle closed over the princess once more, and she did not stir.
You stood on the cold mountain with your sister's hand crushed in yours and the grey morning coming up behind you — free, and ruined, and certain of exactly one thing.
"I'm coming back for you," you said into the wind that could not carry it to her. "Whatever it takes. However long. I am coming back. I promise you — this is not how it ends for now."
— To be continued… —
